coverage: All 17 PDF pages: Sections 1-7.1, Appendices A-D, Tables 1-10, figure captions and references; Figure 2 and Tables 4-6 visually checked.
problem: Separate problematic-question diagnosis from clarification-conditioned SQL generation and explanations of unsupported requests.
method: Defines eight problem categories, generates paired interpretations or unsupported cases, filters them with a three-model council, and simulates style-conditioned dialogue. Ambiguity filtering removes dominant readings; unanswerability means no council-generated valid SQL was found.
evaluation: Eight models, four category-information modes, balanced BIRD/Spider subsets, three clarification turns plus a final response. Execution matching tolerates extra columns; feedback is council-judged. Human audits cover 52 questions and 150 conversations, not the whole dataset.
findings: Oracle categories improve ambiguous execution and refusal feedback, but final SQL remains difficult. Termination after relevant feedback can be high while execution accuracy stays low.
limitations: Council membership overlaps generation, evaluation and tested models. The small human audit reports 75% SQL correctness. Simulated users do not give vague or incorrect clarifications or change intent. For benchmark-unanswerable items, the user simulator refuses clarification requests; this is not a guarantee that the evaluated SQL agent refuses.
relevance: A controlled diagnostic benchmark, not proof of unanswerability or evidence of real-user dialogue reliability.

claims.claim: Generated cases are validated.
claims.evidence: Ten automated filters are used, but the human subset gives 75% SQL correctness and 78.1% feedback accuracy.
claims.disposition: Validation is fallible; do not treat all labels as independently human verified.

claims.evidence: Stage 7 retains cases after the council fails to produce valid SQL; Section 7.1 explicitly acknowledges approximation.
claims.disposition: Operationally unsolved, not formally impossible.

coverage: All 45 pages: main sections 1–6; Appendices A–K, including AmbigSQL construction, all additional results, metrics, action/user-simulator prompts, qualitative failures, hyperparameters and assets.
problem: General conversational tuning does not reliably teach a model when to clarify, and limited conversation data can make action learning brittle.
method: ACT creates contrasting clarify/answer preferences, samples a response from the current policy, simulates its continuation, and replaces a winning or losing trajectory before a DPO update. AmbigSQL adds three synthetic underspecification types to paired Spider requests.
evaluation: Zephyr 7B is tuned with 50, 100 or 250 conversations and compared with SFT, preference baselines and larger prompted models on AmbigSQL, PACIFIC and Abg-CoQA. Separate action metrics and trajectory outcomes distinguish asking from actually solving; SQL outcomes use execution match.
findings: On AmbigSQL with 50 conversations, ACT raises execution match from SFT’s 21.9% to 43.6%; gains shrink at 250 conversations. Larger prompted models still achieve higher SQL execution scores. Ablations on PACIFIC support contributions from action contrast, on-policy sampling and trajectory simulation.
limitations: Ambiguity is synthetically balanced and derived from a known target SQL. The SQL simulator sees that target and is instructed to rephrase the desired request, so measured recovery is not a human interaction study. Preference labels assume clarification timing is appropriate. Performance depends on commercial classifiers/simulators and task-specific outcome heuristics; the appendix reports inconsistent AmbigSQL beta values.
relevance: A concrete learning mechanism and paired benchmark for studying the distinction between recognizing a need to clarify and using clarification to recover an intended SQL query.

claims.claim: Improved clarification is demonstrated with real users.

claims.disposition: Qualify as simulated interaction, not user-study evidence.

coverage: All twelve PDF pages, Sections 1-7, limitations, Appendices A-B, prompts, error examples, tables and figure data/descriptions.
problem: Single or superficially diverse SQL generations can omit plausible readings of ambiguous requests.
method: An anchor proposes an interpretation; adversaries seek alternatives subject to negative constraints and confidence gates. Candidate SQL is generated with execution repair, pruned when results agree, and used to synthesize contrastive clarification questions.
evaluation: AMBROSIA uses 440 test examples; AmbiQT uses a preprocessed validation set. Full-data versus schema-only conditions change generation context, while verification still executes against the full database. Metrics assess interpretation/output coverage, precision and perfect-set matching.
findings: AIR improves schema-only F1 over the reported IntentRL comparison and reduces duplicate outputs. IntentRL retains better full-data AMBROSIA F1 and AmbiQT recall. The paper reports roughly 40 seconds per query for unoptimized serial API calls.
limitations: Different executed outputs prove query divergence only if proposed readings are valid. Identical current-instance results can hide semantic differences. No user study, clarification-quality assessment or cumulative dialogue-success evaluation is performed; fewer outputs are a burden proxy, not measured user effort.
relevance: Separates interpretation discovery from execution-based discrimination, while exposing the difference between coverage and completed clarification.

claims.claim: AIR works without the database.
claims.evidence: Sections 3.1 and 4.2 explicitly retain backend execution and result-grounded synthesis under schema-only generation context.
claims.disposition: Schema-only does not mean database-free.

claims.claim: AIR resolves ambiguity with superior efficiency.

claims.disposition: Report interpretation coverage and candidate economy, not proven user-experience or real-time superiority.

coverage: All 22 pages: sections 1–7, limitations/ethics, algorithm 1, all result and ablation tables, and appendices A–F including prompts and SQL-output examples.
problem: A top-k SQL generator often returns superficial variants of one interpretation instead of covering plausible alternatives.
method: AmbiQT perturbs Spider schemas to construct two references per question across column, table, join and precomputed-aggregate ambiguity. LogicalBeam first generates plans/templates with controlled join/selection-count changes, then restricts infilling branches to schema names; candidates are combined with ordinary beam outputs.
evaluation: BothInTopK and EitherInTopK measure reference coverage among five outputs using execution matching, with exact-set-match results in the appendix. Historical T5, Flan-T5, RESDSQL, ChatGPT and Codex baselines are compared; standard Spider and KaggleDBQA top-five accuracy is also assessed.
findings: Explicit structural and schema diversity increases coverage of both references. Ablations show different contributions by ambiguity type, and unrestricted sampling frequently repeats the same interpretation. The strongest relative gains depend on the chosen baseline and ambiguity category.
limitations: The English-only benchmark is built by controlled schema changes, not observed user interactions. Two references and four transformation families bound coverage; neither user clarification success nor all naturally possible interpretations is measured. Two decoding stages add work and residual alias variants remain.
relevance: A foundational interpretation-coverage benchmark and decoding baseline; top-five oracle coverage must remain separate from selecting the user-intended answer.

claims.claim: LogicalBeam resolves user ambiguity.
claims.evidence: Sections 3 and 6 score whether two constructed SQL references appear among five outputs; no interaction policy is evaluated.
claims.disposition: Supports candidate coverage, not completed user disambiguation.

claims.claim: All components improve every ambiguity type.
claims.evidence: Table 4 improves column/table coverage after schema diversity but decreases join/precomputed-aggregate coverage relative to template-only diversity.
claims.disposition: Component benefits are category-dependent.

coverage: All four PDF pages, Sections 1-4, taxonomy, technical details, demonstration text and Figures 1-3 captions/UI descriptions. No appendices present.
problem: Ambiguous phrases can map to different schema elements or depend on unstated external reasoning choices. The system aims to expose those choices before SQL generation.
method: A seven-type taxonomy separates database/schema/value/operation ambiguity from source, context, premise and reference ambiguity. Prompted detection produces multiple-choice clarification, including free-text Other and skip/Abstain options. A taxonomy-organized preference tree stores replies; later constraints override earlier ones and rewritten queries are checked again.
evaluation: This is a system demonstration integrated with XiYan-SQL, with 40 curated BIRD/TAG examples and customizable queries/databases. The paper illustrates side-by-side query comparison, rather than a controlled aggregate accuracy or user-study evaluation.
findings: The walkthrough shows how user choices modify schema mappings, time constraints and additional filters. It demonstrates an interaction design and state-management mechanism, not general accuracy gains.
limitations: Coverage depends on prompted detection and the supplied taxonomy. Claims that refinement resolves all dependent ambiguities are architectural aims; no formal guarantee, broad benchmark comparison or real-user outcome study establishes them.
relevance: Useful for clarification interfaces and dependent ambiguity handling; its skip option is a user action, distinct from model refusal on an unanswerable request.

claims.claim: Iterative refinement ensures dependent ambiguities are resolved.
claims.evidence: Section 2.4 describes re-running the detector, while Section 3 supplies only a curated demonstration.
claims.disposition: Treat as intended behavior, not an empirical or formal completeness guarantee.

version: arXiv:2406.19073v2, 31 October 2024; NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks paper
coverage: All 29 PDF pages, including checklist and Appendices A-H: generation prompts, database configurations, annotation protocol, evaluation/extraction details, error examples and datasheet. Few-shot plot and annotation-interface figure visually inspected.
problem: Evaluate multiple valid SQL interpretations when linguistic ambiguity persists despite fully available database context.
method: Generates constrained synthetic databases, then elicits human questions and interpretations. Scope/attachment SQL comes from templates; vague-query SQL begins with expert-written queries on simplified schemas. Retains nonempty, distinct interpretation results.
evaluation: 1,277 ambiguous questions, 2,965 resolved interpretations and 846 databases across 16 domains; 10% reserved for demonstrations. Six LLMs use ambiguity prompts or beam outputs with complete schema and data dumps. Micro recall, precision and AllFound score interpretation coverage.
findings: Best zero-shot ambiguous recall is 30.7% and AllFound 1.9% for prompted Llama3-70B; its resolved-input recall is 64.5%. Few-shot examples modestly improve coverage. Attachment is difficult even when resolved, so parser capability also affects results.
limitations: Small synthetic databases and three ambiguity families limit realism. Matching flattens query output into sets of values, allowing occasional false equivalences. Interpretations can remain ambiguous; SQL-aware annotators and templates constrain language. No unanswerability or live clarification policy is evaluated.
relevance: Strong controlled test of interpretation coverage; combine with precision and resolved-input baselines rather than treating AllFound as complete dialogue success.

claims.disposition: Describe relaxed single-database execution matching, not semantic proof.

coverage: All 14 proceedings pages, Sections 1-10, Tables 1-7 and figures/captions; all 4 supplementary pages A.1-A.4 including model substitutions and correction settings.
problem: Annotation errors and underspecified questions can distort both SQL correctness labels and rankings used to compare agents.
method: SAR-Agent probes databases and drafts diagnoses; two authors independently check flagged cases, with consensus adjudication and additional pattern-driven review. SAPAR combines diagnoses with human correction of questions, knowledge, SQL, schema and sometimes database rows.
evaluation: Audits 498 unique BIRD Mini-Dev examples and 121 public-gold Spider2-Snow cases. Re-runs 16 reproducible agents on a random 100-example BIRD subset before and after correction; supplements disclose substituted backend models and four correction settings.
findings: Reports 263/498 and 76/121 examples with annotation issues, including ambiguity. Corrections change agent accuracy and rank; SQL-only correction produces different rankings from fully corrected inputs. Diagnostic precision is measured against human review, not automatic ground truth.
limitations: Spider coverage is a dated public-gold subset, not all 547 tasks or current releases. Agent reruns sometimes substitute models, so they do not exactly reproduce leaderboard configurations. Corrections alter inputs as well as labels; the 100-case reranking is not a corrected full leaderboard, and false-negative recall is not exhaustively established.
relevance: Supports auditing evaluation references and recording ambiguity policies before interpreting reliability or abstention scores.

claims.claim: Benchmark error rates exceed 50%.
claims.evidence: The examined populations are 498 unique Mini-Dev cases using full Dev databases and 121 Spider2-Snow cases with publicly available gold; Spider gold snapshot predates October 2025 corrections.
claims.disposition: Supported for explicitly dated inspected subsets, not all current versions.

claims.disposition: Reevaluated implementations under disclosed configurations, not exact leaderboard-run reproduction.

coverage: All 27 pages including main sections 1–8, limitations and Appendices A–M: Bayesian derivation, proposed extensions, synthesis constraints, schema fixes, candidate generation, error/cost studies, complete annotator tutorial and regex experiment. Interface figures 11–12 visually inspected.
problem: Non-programmers cannot readily inspect complex SQL, yet reliable annotation and intent verification require distinguishing subtly different programs.
method: APEL maintains a prior over candidate SQL equivalence classes, synthesizes small databases that maximize expected information gain, and asks annotators to choose the intended output. Bayesian updates and a learned annotator-error model combine noisy responses. A fuzz-then-drop heuristic trades informativeness against database size.
evaluation: An oracle simulation and a study with 11 university non-programmers evaluate Spider-derived tasks. The human study covers 240 utterances, approximately 2.5 annotators per utterance and up to three questions per annotator. Two authors establish corrected reference annotations using APEL-assisted adjudication; candidate matching uses randomized test suites.
findings: On the corrected human-study reference, APEL reaches 75% annotation accuracy versus the seed parser’s 59%, matching the original Spider labels’ 75%. The candidate ceiling is 88%. Interaction exposes schema misunderstandings, missing zero-count entities and tie-handling errors.
limitations: The result is annotation accuracy, not demonstrated downstream parser training or proven cost superiority over experts. The reference was created with the evaluated framework, and finite random testing only approximates SQL equivalence. Candidate coverage, unnatural synthetic databases, arithmetic burden and vague utterances limit reliability. Explicit unanswerable labeling is not supported.
relevance: A substantive human-tested approach to clarification through concrete counterexamples and to auditing benchmark semantics, especially when natural-language paraphrases hide program differences.

claims.claim: APEL demonstrates cheaper expert-equivalent labeling and better trained parsers.
claims.evidence: The study reports matched annotation accuracy but explicitly states that neither downstream fine-tuning benefit nor comparative annotation cost was empirically validated.
claims.disposition: Limit conclusion to measured annotation accuracy.

claims.evidence: The orchestra/company founding example requires an insufficient-information label, but §6.6 states that neither Spider nor APEL supports that option.
claims.disposition: Distinguish identification in qualitative feedback from supported output behavior.

claims.disposition: Describe SQL equivalence as approximate test-suite agreement.

coverage: All 29 pages: sections 1–6 and appendices A–E, annotation guidelines, schemas, query/data examples, agent/simulator prompts, model tables and eight-person user study; rendered taxonomy/statistics/schema figures inspected.
problem: Database questions can contain several interacting semantic, syntactic, schema and computation choices that conversational clarification handles inefficiently.
method: Structured disambiguation decomposes choices into multiple-choice selectors and threshold sliders. GPT-4.1 proposes questions over six existing databases; authors select, revise and annotate interpretations. A two-stage user simulator identifies relevant ambiguity points before answering.
evaluation: Separate tasks measure ambiguity coverage, exact disambiguation and SQL accuracy with supplied resolutions. End-to-end scoring permits extra output columns and conditions intended queries on non-empty results. The main comparison uses simulator token-based effort; eight participants provide a separate, small within-subject interface evaluation.
findings: Structured interaction achieves similar execution performance with lower simulated effort; participants report lower workload. Incorrect SQL and missed/wrong interpretations remain common. More reasoning helps some configurations but not uniformly.
limitations: Questions are generated and author-curated, not a natural user-log sample. Global conventions remove some choices from ambiguity scoring. Completeness is relative to annotations and LLM alignment. The manuscript inconsistently states 331 versus 311 task instances; benchmark releases must be pinned.
relevance: A useful multi-ambiguity and interface benchmark whose finite choices, numeric vagueness, simulator assumptions and modest human evidence should remain explicit.

claims.disposition: Include numeric parameter selection as well as finite choices.

claims.disposition: Record the discrepancy and pin release versions rather than silently selecting a count.

coverage: All four pages, Sections 1-3, equations, worked example and Figure 1; rendered Figure 1 inspected. No appendices.
problem: Whole-query confidence obscures which predicates, joins or modifiers encode competing interpretations of an underspecified request.
method: Runs several SQL generators, aligns clause-level SQL atoms with question phrases, combines model agreement with a per-user/schema preference matrix, and reranks candidate queries after user choices. Preference counts bias later selections without retraining generator weights.
evaluation: A demonstration scenario uses Spider’s student/pet database and a nine-step interface walkthrough. The paper supplies architecture and arithmetic examples, not a controlled user study, calibration experiment or benchmark comparison.
findings: The interface exposes disagreement and lets users inspect alternatives before choosing a candidate. The paper illustrates how atom and model preferences change ranking.
limitations: Available interpretations are bounded by model-generated candidates; the paper explicitly requires reformulation if none matches intent. Agreement is a heuristic, not empirically calibrated confidence. The displayed SQL tree uses COUNT > 2 while the selected example discusses exactly two, so the walkthrough does not prove semantic consistency of every interface view.
relevance: Useful design for exposing localized ambiguity and recording preferences, with demonstration-level evidence rather than established improvement in user resolution.

claims.disposition: Mechanism illustrated; no measured longitudinal benefit.

claims.disposition: Displayed example has an unresolved representation mismatch; do not infer end-to-end semantic verification.

coverage: All 26 pages, Sections 1-6, Appendices A-C, full synthesis/validation/inference prompts, reward equations, Tables 1-4 and Algorithm 1.
problem: Enterprise SQL generators may force answers despite missing metric definitions, dimensions or user-specified constraints.
method: Mutates business-grounded seed questions into eight tasks, synthesizes target-conditioned rationales, then fine-tunes Qwen3-1.7B with supervised learning and GRPO. Rewards combine SQL execution/structure, response similarity, output format and length.
evaluation: Ent-SQL-Bench is a 1,262-instance held-out sample of the same synthetic enterprise corpus. SQL tasks use execution agreement; clarification/refusal targets use three GPT-4o judgments. Ablations remove auxiliary reward terms while preserving the primary outcome rewards.
findings: The reported macro-average improves after training, including non-SQL response categories. Results support task-conditioned behavior within the studied corpus, without testing user replies or successful clarification-to-SQL completion.
limitations: Target-conditioned rationales are constructed explanations, not evidence of faithful internal reasoning. No cross-domain or independent user study supports general enterprise-readiness claims. Main training descriptions disagree on five versus ten SFT epochs, and the source omits confidence intervals or seed variability for its headline gains.
relevance: Directly relevant boundary-aware training baseline; distinguish its outcome scoring from verified reasoning, interactive recovery and deployment reliability.

claims.claim: Knowledge-grounded synthesis guarantees faithful reasoning.
claims.evidence: Equation 1 generates a rationale conditioned on the target; Section 6 acknowledges intermediate reasoning remains unverified.
claims.disposition: Evidence-anchored rationale supervision, not a demonstrated causal-faithfulness guarantee.

claims.disposition: Response-level clarification/refusal performance only.

claims.disposition: Unresolved reproduction detail; do not present either as the verified executed setting.

version: arXiv v3, 24 March 2026; ICLR 2026 conference paper
coverage: All 49 PDF pages: Sections 1-9, ethics/reproducibility, Appendices A-R, annotation taxonomies, metrics and executable-test examples, simulator design/evaluation and every prompt. Read extracted tables and figure captions; no claim of independently reproducing plotted trajectories.
problem: Static dialogue benchmarks cannot measure an agent choosing what to ask, retrieve or execute when user intent, documentation and database state interact.
method: BIRD-Interact injects recoverable ambiguities into database tasks and adds dependent follow-ups. A function-driven simulator maps requests to annotated clarification, SQL-fragment localization or refusal. Conversational and autonomous protocols impose different action budgets and test executable outcomes.
evaluation: The Full and Lite sets contain 600 and 300 tasks. Seven systems are evaluated per setting in single runs; follow-up success is cumulative. UserSim-Guard tests 2,100 simulator requests. Human alignment compares seven model-level success rates on 100 sampled tasks; dataset-quality review samples 300 items.
findings: Full-set end-to-end agent success reaches 17% for GPT-5. Function-driven simulation improves refusal of inappropriate information requests; GPT-4o simulator scores correlate 0.84 with human-derived model success rates. Additional interaction helps some models, rather than establishing a universal scaling law.
limitations: Unique SQL-grounded clarifications, artificial action costs and expert users constrain realism. UNA concerns privileged or out-of-scope simulator requests, not unanswerable database tasks. Single runs lack variability estimates; finite execution tests do not prove SQL equivalence. Follow-up rates include prior failures.
relevance: Provides a controlled environment for source selection, clarification chains and changing database state, with explicit simulator and evaluation boundaries.

coverage: All 22 PDF pages: Sections 1-10, all controlled/pilot/confirmatory tables and recorded deviations, Appendices A-E, supported policy/schema, reproduction and qualification boundaries.
problem: SQL retained after a business-definition change can execute and match the current snapshot while implementing the wrong requested revision on other admissible data.
method: An explicit profile binds policy revision, report interval and knowledge cutoff to exact monetary semantics and legal synthetic ledgers. Obligation coverage selects counterexamples under a fixed budget; a separate implementation freezes finite-suite labels and replays decisions.
evaluation: Authored mutations establish mechanism behavior; a 24-family pilot uses two local model/runtime bundles and repeated samples. A locally preregistered confirmation uses 32 new authored families, 192 query-definition cells, eight-ledger arms and family-level paired inference. Native tools are qualified separately rather than ranked as full competing systems.
findings: The confirmation detects 137/144 nonconforming cells versus 127/144 with generic ordering; 63 errors agree on the initial snapshot. Current-obligation and equal-weight ablations also detect 137, identifying coverage rather than revision-specific weighting as the measured benefit.
limitations: Approval of policy semantics remains external. The schema, revisions and ledgers are authored; two local bundles do not establish enterprise transfer. Zero rejections of finite-suite-agreeing cases follow the replay/suite relationship and do not prove population false-rejection control. Preregistration timestamps are local, with a disclosed 74-versus-81 candidate-pool deviation; raw artifacts lack a public identifier.
relevance: Clarifies when verification should reject, retain finite evidence or request clarification after semantic change, without treating every historical query as stale.

claims.evidence: Current-obligation and equal-weight scoring match guided detection at the registered eight-ledger budget; target-definition-only pilot coverage also retains the benefit.
claims.disposition: Attribute the observed improvement to obligation coverage; do not claim added benefit from revision-specific weighting.

claims.evidence: Agreeing labels are finite-suite labels; selected checking ledgers are included in that suite, and replayable legal discrepancies define rejection. The paper explicitly separates this from full-domain conformance.
claims.disposition: Report bounded empirical agreement and witness soundness conditional on evaluator/legality assumptions.

coverage: All 26 PDF pages, including proof, curation examples, sensitivity analyses, content-aware policy criteria, and all QA/SQL generation and judging prompts in Appendices A-E. Figure 4 visually inspected.
problem: Separate ambiguity admitted by an input from valid answers accessible to a particular model.
method: Enumerates candidate answers, generates an answer-conditioned clarification for each, and retains candidates consistently recovered when re-answering. The formal clarification-answer bijection assumes faithful, unique clarifications exist for every valid answer.
evaluation: Four models on 1,000 AmbigQA questions, 100 curated AmbigQA-HQ questions and 96 ambiguous AMBROSIA requests. SQL uses five enumerations and five recoveries; GPT-5.4-mini groups and judges semantic equivalence. Model-specific references are also recovery-filtered.
findings: Set-F1 leads in seven of twelve model/dataset settings, including two of four SQL settings. Filtering chiefly improves precision at some recall cost. Answer/clarify/abstain and ambiguity-detection experiments are QA-only.
limitations: Cycle consistency can preserve factual errors; missed proposals cannot be recovered. Reference construction shares the recovery criterion and semantic judge with the estimator. The policy labels ANSWER when only one interpretation is model-accessible, even if the world admits others; this is not a user-intent safety guarantee.
relevance: Offers a model-dependent ambiguity estimator, with direct SQL answer-set evidence but no SQL dialogue-policy or end-user validation.

coverage: All 33 pages: sections 1–7; Appendices A–D; all taxonomy/conversation examples, Algorithms 1–9, complete supplied generation/evaluation prompts, Tables 1–26 and reported confidence intervals.
problem: Binary ambiguity detection can hide failure to identify the actual schema elements involved, particularly when a request contains more than one ambiguous reference and clarification is incomplete.
method: CLARITY extracts SQL-grounded targets, retrieves competing columns or values, generates pivot terms and rewritten questions, and filters them with multiple LLM evaluators. It synthesizes concise, verbose, partial and unhelpful conversation variants and retains pivot-to-target annotations for diagnostic evaluation.
evaluation: Spider- and BIRD-derived instances support alternative-SQL prediction, conversation-conditioned SQL generation, and AmbiSQL detection/localization assessment. Three experts validate a stratified 448-instance sample by majority vote. Five LLMs are tested; exemplars with metadata are supplied only in context, not as test labels.
findings: Binary detection is often high while target matching and complete interpretation recovery remain much lower. GPT-5 multi-facet strict exact match increases markedly with metadata-bearing exemplars, but gains and rankings vary by model, category and dataset.
limitations: Conversation-to-SQL evaluation supplies the completed dialogue, so it does not measure a deployed agent choosing and adapting its own questions. Schema-linkability definitions cover a narrower notion than general SQL answerability; an absent value need not make a query semantically invalid. Generated labels and human checks do not prove exhaustive interpretation coverage. The prose excludes value-level SQL evaluation while result tables include value-ambiguity columns, leaving protocol scope unresolved.
relevance: Useful for diagnosing the gap between detecting ambiguity and locating or resolving its sources, with controlled multi-facet stress tests rather than unrestricted real-user interaction.

claims.claim: The reported multi-turn scores measure an agent conducting live clarification.
claims.evidence: Models receive the full conversation except final SQL and generate one resolved query; the evaluation prompt confirms this fixed-dialogue protocol.
claims.disposition: Qualify as conversation-conditioned SQL prediction.

claims.claim: Unanswerability establishes that no valid SQL query exists in the general sense.
claims.evidence: The taxonomy defines it by lack of a column/value mapping; examples mark an absent card-type value unanswerable. No general logical or operational impossibility procedure is provided.
claims.disposition: Scope to the benchmark’s schema/value-linkability convention.

claims.disposition: Flag internal protocol inconsistency; avoid claiming comprehensive or uniformly excluded value-level SQL evaluation.

coverage: All 35 PDF pages: main Sections 1-4, availability and ethics, Appendices A-C, all questionnaire items and 45 fixed questions, statistical formulas, model selection and post-study correctness analysis. Visually inspected interface screenshot on PDF page 27.
problem: Clinical SQL benchmark accuracy alone cannot show whether practitioners can express information needs, resolve misunderstandings or trust an interface appropriately.
method: Fourteen physicians compare single-turn and conversational GPT-5.4 interfaces over the 100-patient MIMIC-IV Demo in a randomized-order, counterbalanced within-subject study. Fixed selected questions precede free exploration; questionnaires measure usability, acceptance and perceived trust.
evaluation: SUS and UTAUT comparisons use paired tests. Dialogue coding pools 425 user turns from 21 professionals including two pilots with changing models/procedures. A separate post-study review judges 186 evaluable SQL-generating turns from 57 main-study conversational sessions against gold answers or complete dialogue context.
findings: Mean SUS rises from 68.2 to 85.9. Free questions prompt clarification on 40/161 conversational turns versus 1/56 predefined turns; 27/42 episodes involve clinical or EHR knowledge. Study designers judge 134/186 conversational outputs correct, with errors involving entity matching, population/aggregation and cross-turn propagation.
limitations: Fourteen main participants, one small demo database and strong prior conversational-AI familiarity limit generalization. Trigger frequency measures this agent’s behavior rather than independently adjudicated ambiguity prevalence. Pooled pilots differ from the main protocol; post-study correctness is not a matched interface accuracy comparison. Trust remains self-reported.
relevance: Adds rare practitioner evidence and concrete ambiguity categories while exposing a gap between satisfaction and verified conversational correctness.

claims.disposition: Call it observed clarification frequency, not population prevalence or a causal effect.

coverage: All substantive Sections 1-8 on PDF pages 1-9, equations 1-3, Figure 1, Tables 1-6; remaining pages are references. No appendices in this version.
problem: Output diversity may reflect legitimate interpretation differences or unreliable generation under one interpretation; these require different interventions.
method: CLUES builds interpretation and answer similarity matrices plus provenance links. Heat-kernel entropy measures ambiguity; a regularized Schur complement with PSD projection yields an operational conditional-instability score. Median splits define four routing regimes.
evaluation: Open QA uses gold interpretations. The clinical study uses 109 questions, five models and four temperatures, with controlled interpretations followed by a generated-interpretation deployment configuration. Answers and similarities are judged by LLMs; clinical SQL runs on a restricted Optum database.
findings: Conditional instability improves pooled known-interpretation clinical AUROC from 0.600 to 0.762. In the deployment setup its AUROC is 0.648 versus 0.687 for result entropy, a nonsignificant difference. The compound regime contains 48 of 95 failures across pooled configurations.
limitations: Generated interpretations, similarity judgments, thresholds and repeated model/question instances shape the results. Routing is analyzed retrospectively; benefits of actual clarification or human review are not tested. Section 5.2 alternately describes a gold interpretation plus three alternatives and a three-interpretation/nine-query setup.
relevance: Provides diagnostic separation rather than a validated clinical safety or automatic-routing guarantee.

claims.claim: CLUES improves failure prediction.
claims.evidence: Known-interpretation pooled clinical AUROC improves, but deployment HR|I is 0.648 versus HR 0.687, p=0.20.
claims.disposition: Restrict superiority to the known-interpretation setting; deployment advantage is diagnostic granularity.

claims.claim: Regime routing catches half of errors.
claims.evidence: Table 6 retrospectively places 48/95 failures in a roughly quarter-sized group; no intervention is evaluated.
claims.disposition: Error concentration supports a routing hypothesis, not demonstrated review/clarification effectiveness.

claims.claim: Clinical interpretation sample count is unambiguous.
claims.evidence: Section 5.2 says a gold-matching interpretation plus three alternatives but then specifies 3×3=9 queries.
claims.disposition: Unresolved reporting inconsistency; avoid a precise interpretation-count claim.

version: CPAL 2026 proceedings, PMLR 328:940–956; publisher-linked 17-page PDF, titled Concept based Ambiguity Resolution in LLMs.
coverage: All 17 PDF pages: Sections 1–5, references and Appendices A–E; all equations, Algorithm 1, Table 1 and Figures 1–11 with captions/examples. Figure-dependent entropy, detection, API-retrieval and distance-pattern results on PDF pages 5, 9, 10, 14 and 15 were visually inspected.
problem: Models may repeatedly produce one reading of an ambiguous request, leaving ordinary embedding similarity or sampled agreement insensitive to alternative interpretations.
method: Few-shot examples encourage two interpretations. Sparse-autoencoder features supply masked concept representations for an approximate path-kernel distance, using straight-line interpolation from zero to final weights rather than the original training path. A separate supervised concept predictor retrieves API calls.
evaluation: Ambiguity detection uses AMBROSIA questions and generated interpretations treated as unambiguous controls. Distances are compared with dense embeddings; the classification threshold is the intersection of the plotted class-density curves. A 20-question activation study and a separate Gorilla TensorFlow Hub retrieval experiment provide supporting evidence.
findings: The paper reports 86.25% detection accuracy versus 70% and 77.75% for dense-distance baselines in this constructed comparison. Targeted activation improves aggregate self-judgment but decreases ambiguous-class accuracy. The best concept-retrieval variant slightly exceeds the compared fine-tuned Gorilla API-call result, while domain accuracy remains lower.
limitations: A held-out threshold-selection protocol, independent validation of generated negative labels and repeated-run uncertainty are not clearly reported. Internal activations and model-specific SAEs are required. Limited activation examples support a mechanism hypothesis, not a universal explanation of ambiguity. No SQL execution, active clarification, refusal or user-outcome evaluation is provided.
relevance: Directly relevant to pre-generation ambiguity detection for database questions; its API-retrieval result should remain separate from claims about SQL generation or resolving a user’s intended interpretation.

claims.claim: The paper establishes improved Text-to-SQL answer accuracy.
claims.evidence: Section 4.1 measures ambiguity classification from AMBROSIA question/interpretation distances; Section 4.2 measures API domain and API-call retrieval. No generated-SQL execution or clarification outcome metric is reported.
claims.disposition: Restrict the SQL contribution to ambiguity detection rather than answer accuracy or completed resolution.

claims.claim: The 86.25% figure establishes held-out general ambiguity-detection performance.
claims.evidence: Generated interpretations are treated as unambiguous questions; the threshold is chosen at the intersection of the plotted ambiguous/unambiguous density curves. The paper does not clearly describe separate threshold-fitting and test sets or independent validation of these controls.
claims.locator: Section 4.1, PDF pages 8–9; Figure 5; Appendix B.1
claims.disposition: Report as a result under the constructed evaluation protocol, with unresolved threshold and label-validation boundaries.

claims.claim: Activating missing concepts improves recognition of ambiguous inputs uniformly.
claims.evidence: Table 1 increases unambiguous accuracy from 39.8% to 60.5% but decreases ambiguous accuracy from 59.3% to 42.8%; the stated class ratio is two unambiguous examples per ambiguous example.
claims.locator: Appendix B.3 and Table 1, PDF pages 15–16
claims.disposition: Distinguish aggregate improvement from the trade-off between detecting ambiguity and rejecting false alarms.

version: AAAI 2025 proceedings; linked arXiv:2501.09527v1 supplies Appendices A-H
coverage: All nine proceedings PDF pages and experimental Appendices A-H in the 15-page extended version, including tables and plot captions. Extended Figures 7–10 visually inspected.
problem: Detect erroneous SQL and unsupported requests under domain, compositional and answerability shifts.
method: Uses token-entropy or sequence-probability scores with thresholding, logistic regression or Gaussian-mixture selection, and compares post-hoc Platt/isotonic calibration. A known portion of shifted data is used for fitting.
evaluation: T5, Llama 3 and GPT-based DAIL-SQL are tested on English PAUQ cross-database, template and length splits plus EHRSQL; execution match labels errors.
findings: Rejection often catches unanswerable inputs more readily than wrong SQL for relevant questions. Calibration improves, especially for T5; strong shift can make rejection discard many correct answers.
limitations: Fitting on known shifted examples differs from deployment without labeled target data. The paper uses task-specific risk/coverage and Result EX definitions; its plotted error-detection gains should not be presented as universal conditional-risk guarantees.
relevance: Shows why answerability detection and incorrect-generation detection need separate reporting, even when they share a confidence score.

claims.claim: Rejection improves reliability.
claims.evidence: Section 4 and Appendix D show reduced returned errors alongside substantial correct-answer rejection under template and length shifts.
claims.disposition: Supported as a trade-off, not a free accuracy improvement.

claims.claim: The classifier detects unsupported questions better than wrong SQL.
claims.evidence: Appendix F/Figure 8 separates NULL and SQL error classes; their detection behavior differs across models.
claims.disposition: Retain the distinction and evaluated-model scope.

version: arXiv:2508.14056v1 author manuscript, 16 pages including supplement; AAAI 2026 bibliographic record independently matched
coverage: Entire manuscript and supplementary prompts, Tables 1-4, examples and figure captions; rendered Table 1/Figure 3 inspected. Publisher endpoint returned non-PDF content, so published-version differences were not established.
problem: SQL users need estimates of candidate correctness without knowing the reference query, especially when model internals are restricted.
method: Compares verbal self-report, repeated-generation agreement by execution/embedding/schema, and token-probability aggregation. SQL-Aware Confidence filters or folds syntactic alternatives and emphasizes meaningful SQL tokens; execution feedback supplies another signal.
evaluation: Spider and BIRD development queries, multiple proprietary and open-weight generators, AUROC and expected calibration error. Ablations vary aggregation, SQL-specific normalization and execution grounding; appendix supplies prompts and case analyses.
findings: SAC-Product leads on Spider and SAC-Average on BIRD in the reported table. Execution consistency is strongest among tested black-box approaches, with extra sampling/execution cost. Performance depends on query length and schema-token composition.
limitations: The favorable aggregation differs by benchmark. Result agreement on a database and confidence normalization do not prove semantic equivalence or identify ambiguous intent. Some experimental descriptions and supplemental model inventories differ; exact snapshots, execution-grounding implementation and significance procedures need more detail for reproduction.
relevance: A source of candidate-confidence baselines and cost/access trade-offs for abstention pipelines; it does not itself evaluate an ambiguity-resolution dialogue.

claims.claim: Average aggregation is generally the best syntax-aware choice.
claims.evidence: Table 1 favors SAC-Product on Spider but SAC-Average on BIRD across the listed models.
claims.disposition: Qualify by dataset rather than universally prefer average.

claims.claim: Execution grounding improves confidence.
claims.evidence: Table 4 shows substantial BIRD SAC gains, small Spider gains and unchanged augmented-CoT results.
claims.locator: Supplementary Table 4 and Detailed Impact of Execution Feedback
claims.disposition: Supported for specified methods; not every method improves.

version: UAI 2025 publisher PDF, 16 pages including supplementary material; proceedings record identifies PMLR 286
coverage: Sections 1-6, Algorithm 1, Tables 1-3, all supplementary text A.1-A.5/B and figure captions. Rendered Figures 10–12 inspected.
problem: Consistency-based confidence assumes that correct generations agree more than incorrect ones, but the assumption has several inequivalent meanings.
method: Defines Sim-Correct, Sim-Separate and label-free Sim-Any hypotheses using pairwise or aggregated similarities. Repeated random grouping and one-sided mean tests measure the fraction of groups supporting each hypothesis; geometric and harmonic aggregators provide confidence scores.
evaluation: Eight QA, summarization and SQL datasets. SQL experiments use Spider, Spider-Realistic and BIRD, with CodeLlama and fine-tuned DeepSeek, and label correctness by execution-result agreement. Confidence experiments report AUROC/AUARC using five random half-dataset evaluations.
findings: Positive aggregate separation supports consistency as a useful ranking signal in the studied settings. Stronger label-aware statements are not directly usable at inference; practical Sim-Any support varies with model, metric, sampling and group size.
limitations: Dataset/group significance does not guarantee a correct individual answer. SQL labels inherit reference and single-database limitations; the learned-model comparison also changes model family and fine-tuning, limiting causal attribution to fine-tuning. Ranking metrics do not establish calibrated per-instance probabilities.
relevance: Provides diagnostic tests and simple confidence baselines for selective SQL generation, rather than a detector of missing information or user ambiguity.

claims.claim: Consistency hypotheses justify confidence estimation.
claims.evidence: Group-level support declines toward individual queries; Table 2 shows improved ranking metrics, not an instance certificate.
claims.locator: Sections 3-5, Figure 4, Table 2 and Appendix A
claims.disposition: Supported as conditional empirical evidence; preserve model/dataset dependence.

claims.claim: Fine-tuning weakens consistency.
claims.evidence: The comparison is CodeLlama few-shot versus a different DeepSeek model fine-tuned on Spider.
claims.disposition: Observed configuration difference; not an isolated causal effect of fine-tuning.

coverage: All 18 PDF pages including sections 1–8, appendices A.1–A.3, dialogue examples and rendered interface/graph figures 4–11.
problem: Database conversations include context switches, ambiguity, unsupported questions and the need to explain returned results.
method: Crowd workers explore database tables while SQL-trained student experts execute queries, assign dialogue acts, clarify requests and describe results. Reference goals encourage connected exploration; subsequent review revises labels, queries and wording.
evaluation: The corpus separates databases across train/dev/test. Tasks are SQL-grounded dialogue-state tracking, description generation for successful SQL and user-dialogue-act prediction. Clarifications are supplied in tracking context after user affirmation; clarification quality itself is not evaluated.
findings: Original baselines struggle with SQL interaction accuracy and distinguishing important acts despite high overall act accuracy. Template responses score worse on BLEU yet better on human logical correctness, showing that fluency metrics can miss semantic errors.
limitations: These are curated Wizard-of-Oz exchanges, not autonomous live-agent conversations. Users see database content and follow reference goals. INFER_SQL/CANNOT_ANSWER are operational annotation categories, not formal proofs of SQL inexpressibility. Historical baseline scores should not describe current models.
relevance: Foundational recorded interaction data, especially valuable when distinguishing supplied clarification context from active clarification-policy evaluation.

claims.claim: CoSQL evaluates autonomous clarification quality.
claims.evidence: Section 5 explicitly excludes that task and gives recorded clarification turns to dialogue-state tracking; conclusion leaves effective clarification to future work.
claims.disposition: Not supported; describe recorded clarification and act prediction.

claims.claim: Response BLEU captures semantic faithfulness.
claims.evidence: Table 6 gives template LCR 41% versus pointer-generator 35%, although BLEU is 9.3 versus 15.1.
claims.disposition: The reported comparison supports separating surface similarity from logical correctness.

version: arXiv:2310.18742v1, 28 October 2023; manuscript labeled Table Representation Learning Workshop at NeurIPS 2023
coverage: All seven PDF pages: Sections 1-4, Table 1, Figure 1 panels and captions, limitations and references. No supplement or appendix in the PDF.
problem: A correctly interpreted question can still yield wrong SQL when the model misunderstands value formats, table coverage or row granularity.
method: The authors manually document two KaggleDBQA databases and clarify query terms/output schemas using supplied reference answers. They vary documentation content and query disambiguation separately, selecting relevant columns to reduce prompt redundancy.
evaluation: GPT-4 with an 8K context is evaluated on 45 Soccer/Crime questions, only two of KaggleDBQA’s eight databases. Exact-match evaluation is manually checked for equivalent formulations; the authors also repair inconsistent or faulty reference answers.
findings: With queries already clarified, schema-only accuracy is 57.8% and full documentation reaches 86.7%: a 28.9-percentage-point gain. The original-question/schema-only condition is 26.7%, so these are different comparisons.
limitations: This is a small manually curated study. Gold-answer-guided documentation and question rewriting approximate oracle assistance, and missing-value semantics are left unresolved. No general automatic documentation or interactive clarification system is evaluated.
relevance: Shows why omitted data semantics should be distinguished from linguistic ambiguity and model generation errors.

claims.claim: Documentation improves performance by 28.9%.
claims.evidence: Figure 1a compares 57.8% with 86.7% under already disambiguated queries.
claims.disposition: Report percentage points with the controlled query condition, not an unrestricted relative gain.

claims.claim: The reported accuracy for data documentation plus output schema is consistent across the paper.
claims.evidence: Figure 1b prints 64.4%; Section 3.2 prose prints 64.6%.
claims.disposition: Minor within-paper reporting mismatch; omit this exact figure from the catalog rather than silently reconcile it.

coverage: All 11 PDF pages: Sections 1-6, equations, Tables 1-5, Figures 1-4 and references. Human-evaluation table and preference plot visually checked.
problem: Repair a base parser's SQL through short validation questions understandable without SQL expertise.
method: A hierarchical RNN predicts error category, token span and replacement choices. Training dialogues reverse synthetic query mutations; the simulator consults reference SQL. The interface uses table headers rather than cell contents.
evaluation: WikiSQL query-match accuracy, dialogue length and question token count; a separate 100-question development sample is evaluated with three user judgments per dialogue.
findings: Five-choice interaction raises SQLNet test query-match accuracy from 61.3% to 69.0%. On the smaller human-study sample, baseline, simulated-user and real-user scores are 58%, 75% and 65%, respectively.
limitations: Single-table WikiSQL and template-based interaction limit transfer. Ideal reference-aware feedback overestimates real-user performance; users can reject all offered choices, and headers may not resolve value meanings.
relevance: An early interactive repair baseline with actual human evidence, but not an ambiguity taxonomy or refusal benchmark.

claims.claim: Interaction improves query generation.
claims.evidence: Table 3 supports the simulated test gain; Table 5 supports a smaller gain with real users on a different 100-question sample.
claims.disposition: Supported within distinct protocols; do not conflate human and simulator scores.

claims.claim: Source code is available.
claims.evidence: Section 5.2 links the author repository; current repository lists only a README.
claims.locator: Section 5.2; official GitHub file listing checked 2026-11-09
claims.disposition: Paper link verified, implementation release not established.

coverage: All substantive Sections 1-8 and Appendices A-G, Tables 1-9, prompts, training details, examples and figure captions. Reference-list text is not treated as evidence for cited papers.
problem: LLMs repeatedly choose preferred readings and omit alternative meanings of ambiguous database questions.
method: Prompts an initial interpretation set, trains a LoRA infilling model on missing readings, then parses each reading with a separate SQL model. Training targets use execution-based matching between generated interpretations and annotated SQL; infilling adds interpretations without removing incorrect initial ones.
evaluation: AmbiQT with empty-result cases filtered out, AMBROSIA transfer, and a separately re-split AMBROSIA training experiment. Reports single/full reference-interpretation coverage, precision and recall; ablates interpretation generators and parser strength.
findings: Infilling improves coverage over initial prompting and transfers better than the tested in-domain end-to-end fine-tuning baseline. Full AMBROSIA coverage remains 18.8%, with 24.2% precision; end-to-end fine-tuning achieves higher full coverage in several in-domain settings.
limitations: Coverage is relative to annotated readings and database execution, not all possible meanings. Unambiguous evaluation does not penalize extra queries. Parser errors and unfiltered interpretations propagate; single-run training and dataset conventions limit generalization claims.
relevance: A modular interpretation-coverage baseline for clarification systems, but generating alternatives does not select actual user intent or prove faithful disambiguation.

claims.claim: Disambiguate-first improves coverage universally.
claims.evidence: Table 1 improves over prompting, but in-domain SFT full coverage 63.2 exceeds 53.2; Table 6 Ambrosia* end-to-end 66.4 exceeds 30.5.
claims.disposition: Distinguish transfer advantages and single-coverage gains from in-domain full-coverage performance.

claims.claim: The method also handles unambiguous questions.
claims.evidence: Table 5 scores whether gold SQL is found and explicitly does not penalize extra queries.
claims.disposition: Supports retrieval of the correct reading, not low false-ambiguity rate.

coverage: All 39 pages: sections 1–8, use/ethics/reproducibility statements, references and Appendices A–L including every task card, prompt, metric definition and numeric table. All four figures visually inspected.
problem: Selecting a plausible database does not ensure that all required sources, cross-database dependencies and executable local contributions have been recovered.
method: DSABench composes executable source units into hidden contracts, then renders and reviews requests. RouteEnv exposes catalog evidence through opaque source identifiers. Scores separate exact source recovery, topology/dependencies, local execution and their conjunction; interactive tasks use two equally weighted latent branches.
evaluation: The 815 tasks include 618 jointly multi-source and 105 interactive tasks, but only 22 sequential dependencies. Seven backends support a routing study; four support a 72-configuration factorial study. Clarification is evaluated through a one-question semantic-slot simulator.
findings: Clarification improves exact branch-source recovery by about 40–43 points. Router-local requests improve individual source execution but do not consistently improve complete workflow success. The best non-privileged clarified conjunction is 16.99%, selected descriptively from the evaluated grid.
limitations: RA-Graph includes a behavior-label gate, and Never Ask’s zero interactive conjunction is partly due to that gate, not universal SQL failure. Preserved examples omit gold constraints from visible wording. Review agreement cannot be reconstructed; evidence/compute schedules differ, and corpus-specific comparators differ. The workflow score does not evaluate final prose answers or unrestricted dialogue.
relevance: Useful for studying ambiguity that changes which database should be queried, and for separating source-set errors, information transfer and local-query failures while preserving benchmark validity boundaries.

claims.claim: 723 tasks require multiple databases jointly.
claims.evidence: The 723 multi-entry target lists include 105 alternative-branch tasks; only 618 require joint source participation.
claims.disposition: Correct joint-versus-alternative source counts.

claims.claim: Never Ask’s zero interactive end-to-end score means every SQL result was wrong.
claims.evidence: Its TEA is 6.94–9.33%, but RA-Graph requires the interactive label even for a singleton source; this gate drives the conjunction toward zero.
claims.disposition: Qualify composite-score mechanism.

claims.claim: Human review guarantees that visible requests specify all executable targets.
claims.evidence: Appendix H.6 documents absent trial-eligibility and LIMIT 5 constraints; B.9 says agreement and final review-coverage distribution cannot be reconstructed.
claims.disposition: Qualify task-validity and annotation evidence.

version: Findings of ACL 2023, pages 5701-5714; proceedings PDF title uses “Unanswerable”, while the Anthology landing record uses “Unknown”
coverage: All fourteen PDF pages, Sections 1-7, limitations, Appendices A-C, error examples and checklist; Tables 1-11 and figure data/captions read.
problem: A parser may emit plausible SQL despite missing or ambiguous concepts in a question/table pair.
method: A six-category analysis motivates NoisySP, but generation mainly edits schemas to create column ambiguity and missing-column cases. DTE combines BERT concept prediction, grounding and CRF span labeling using SQL-derived weak supervision, then instantiates explanation templates.
evaluation: Experiments use NoisySP with WikiSQL and SQL-annotated WTQ, plus a separate 3,000-question commercial failure sample. Metrics assess token-label and grounding accuracy. A separate WTQ experiment measures ordinary answerable-query SQL accuracy.
findings: DTE improves problematic-span labeling and grounding over adapted heuristics/ETA. Reported realistic-data AMB and UNK label accuracies are 75.2% and 70.2%. Most analyzed residual errors involve span boundaries, and SQL gains on ordinary WTQ are small.
limitations: The 20% problematic-question estimate comes from collected failed requests, not an unbiased rate over all user traffic. Synthetic training principally covers two of six categories. Missing values and unsupported calculations follow operational product conventions; these are not universal proofs of unanswerability. Complete clarification-to-SQL success is not evaluated.
relevance: Separates detection, localization and explanation, making it a useful pre-generation diagnostic baseline.

claims.claim: About 20% of real-world questions are problematic.
claims.evidence: Section 2 samples around 3,000 failed commercial requests and then identifies problematic cases.
claims.disposition: Keep the failure-enriched sampling frame; do not generalize prevalence to all traffic.

claims.claim: The approach handles all six categories uniformly.
claims.evidence: Section 3 targets column ambiguity/unanswerability; Appendix C discusses other categories and separate remedies.
claims.disposition: Distinguish taxonomy scope from generated-data and evaluated mechanism scope.

coverage: All 23 pages: main sections 1–9; Appendices A–J with all repeated-run tables, qualitative failures, expert-review description, schema tree and complete displayed synthesis/verification/refinement/user prompts. Figure 3–4 visually inspected.
problem: SQL translation benchmarks often miss the dialogue management and database-state consequences of a user pursuing a multi-step goal involving updates, inserts or deletions.
method: DySQL-Bench synthesizes instructions and reference actions from relational data serialized as logic trees, then applies model validation, instruction backfilling, execution checks and reported expert review. A simulated user, evaluated agent and SQLite environment interact; task success compares final database-state hashes against reference execution.
evaluation: The paper reports 1,072 tasks across 13 databases, divides them by reference-action length, and tests multiple models with a 30-turn cap. Pass^k measures all k sampled runs succeeding, alongside per-domain accuracy, dialogue length, failed SQL calls and a marker-based fabricated-result diagnostic.
findings: The reported GPT-4o score drops from 58.34% overall to 23.81% under Pass^5. Some models produce largely executable SQL yet fail the task, while others repeat or fabricate tool results. Few-shot examples yield modest gains in three tested domains.
limitations: The simulator dynamically responds toward an original fully parameterized instruction, so this is not unrestricted changing-goal evaluation. Final-state equality does not itself validate every conversational answer or intermediate action. Expert review is author-reported and cannot establish error-free data. Short/long counts total 1,062 rather than the stated 1,072. Performance uses one simulator family, and model-size or post-training explanations are observational.
relevance: A valuable adjacent testbed for stateful interaction, correction and repeated-run reliability, with a scoring boundary distinct from semantic equivalence of every SQL statement or user response.

claims.claim: Expert review proves all tasks are perfectly correct.
claims.evidence: §3.3 and Appendix H report full-scope review by ten experts and agreement after consensus, but this is not independent verification or a proof of absence of annotation errors.
claims.disposition: Report the review procedure as an author claim; remove the older catalog wording that describes this version as sampled validation.

claims.claim: The simulator changes the underlying user goal without restriction.
claims.evidence: §4 says it responds to agent outputs to fulfill the original instruction; generation/refinement prompts require all SQL parameters in that instruction.
claims.disposition: Qualify to dynamic dialogue toward a task-defined goal.

claims.claim: The stated short/long breakdown reconciles with 1,072 tasks.
claims.evidence: §3.4 reports 561 Short and 501 Long tasks, totaling 1,062; the Figure 3 domain totals are likewise 354+405+303=1,062.
claims.disposition: Flag count inconsistency; retain 1,072 only as the stated headline until released artifacts reconcile the counts.

version: arXiv:2301.07695v6, 4 March 2026; original NeurIPS 2022 dataset paper
coverage: All 34 pages: Sections 1–5; supplementary datasheet A, complete question/time templates B, SQL assumptions C, preprocessing D, paraphrasing E, splits F, training G, qualitative analysis H and author statement I; all tables and captions.
problem: Hospital staff need temporal and cohort queries beyond fixed interfaces, including requests that cannot be answered from the available EHR schema.
method: Turns a 222-person hospital poll into question templates, manually labels SQL for MIMIC-III/eICU, combines temporal/value slots and human/machine paraphrases, and adds held-out unanswerable requests. Processed databases shuffle patient-associated records, shift time and add synthetic costs.
evaluation: T5 baselines use entropy-based rejection; question templates are shared across train/validation/test while paraphrases differ. Unanswerable questions occur only in validation/test at 33%; a percentile baseline uses that prevalence explicitly.
findings: Rejection improves execution precision but leaves coverage/error trade-offs. Cross-domain transfer is difficult; most EHRSQL queries cannot be parsed by the compared Spider grammar. Some ambiguous questions are folded into the unanswerable pool rather than separately resolved.
limitations: One-hospital question source, two databases and shared templates limit transfer claims. Temporal labels include artificial assumptions, such as diagnosis time equaling admission time in MIMIC-III. Shuffled records and synthetic costs make the dataset unsuitable for clinical inference or outcome analysis.
relevance: Core healthcare answerability benchmark with explicit temporal semantics and access requirements; benchmark precision is not evidence of clinical safety.

claims.claim: Held-out evaluation measures generalization to new question types.
claims.evidence: Section 4.1 and Appendix F require every question template in each split, with paraphrase separation; unanswerables appear only in evaluation.
claims.disposition: Paraphrase/value generalization within templates, not unseen-template generalization.

claims.claim: EHRSQL directly reflects clinical record semantics.
claims.evidence: Appendices C-D specify shifted/shuffled records, synthetic costs and assumed diagnosis/procedure times.
claims.disposition: Query benchmark over processed data, not clinical analysis.

claims.claim: Ambiguity is absent from the benchmark.
claims.evidence: Section 3.1.1 retains filtered utterances as unanswerable; Appendix B.1 explicitly says unanswerables can contain ambiguous questions.
claims.disposition: Ambiguity is included within the refusal category, without separate clarification evaluation.

coverage: All 11 pages: sections 1–6, limitations, figures 1–2, tables 1–3, references and Appendix A fact-sheet template.
problem: Clinical database QA must reject unsupported questions and incorrect SQL instead of optimizing answerable-only generation accuracy.
method: The shared task adapts EHRSQL templates to MIMIC-IV Demo, regenerates paraphrases with manual checking, adds TrustSQL-derived negatives and reserves unseen question templates for validation/test.
evaluation: Eight teams are compared using execution-based Reliability Score. Correct answers and correct refusals earn one; abstaining on answerable questions earns zero; wrong answers or answering unsupported questions incur a configurable penalty. The principal ranking uses penalty 10; an abstain-all baseline scores about 20 on evaluation splits.
findings: Unified LLM methods lead this particular leaderboard. Every submitted system loses to abstain-all under the most severe penalty, illustrating that high moderate-penalty scores still allow errors. This comparison does not isolate architecture from model strength, training or ensembling.
limitations: Data cover a 100-patient demo schema and selected question templates; preprocessing removes duplicate values to reduce ambiguity. Table 1 gives 450 negatives among 5,124 training samples, about 8.8%, compared with approximately 20% in validation and test.
relevance: A useful clinical abstention protocol whose denominator, penalty and schema preprocessing must accompany reported reliability.

claims.claim: Unanswerable-question prevalence is equal across all splits.
claims.evidence: Table 1 lists training 450/5124, validation 232/1163 and test 233/1167. Section 3.5 discusses adding new unanswerable questions exclusively to validation and test before describing their 20% proportions.
claims.disposition: Use the split-specific counts; the 20% description applies to evaluation splits.

claims.claim: Winning systems are reliable under all penalties.

problem: Determine SQL equivalence while exposing the transformations and schema assumptions that justify a positive decision.

relevance: Useful for reference-SQL evaluation, conditional on trusted rules and schema constraints; it cannot verify that a reference captures user intent.

problem: Aggregate Text-to-SQL accuracy mixes model failures, incomplete or inaccurate benchmark inputs and labels, and biases in approximate SQL matching. These sources can require different remedies.
method: The paper organizes limitations into solution, evaluation-data, and evaluation-metric categories. It illustrates ambiguity from projection, filters, duplicate handling and schema information, then uses multiple LLM-generated query variants and disagreement to prioritize manual inspection.
evaluation: The evidence is an illustrative inspection of Spider examples and state-of-the-art systems, rather than a controlled comparison of a new detector. Appendix A lists 43 likely inaccurate-label examples and another 42 examples with other data issues.
findings: A valid alternative interpretation may be penalized by a single reference, while match-function relaxations can accept incorrect predictions. The paper distinguishes genuine unanswerability and false presuppositions from ordinary generation failure and documents errors hidden by one database instance.
limitations: The example lists are explicitly incomplete, and model disagreement is a screening proxy rather than validated automatic error detection. Reported suspicious-example counts are not prevalence estimates for production data. Some examples depend on interpretation conventions; the taxonomy is not claimed complete.
relevance: Provides a useful vocabulary for designing ambiguity and abstention evaluation: state the allowed interpretations, available schema information and comparator behavior, and separate missing predictions from erroneous evaluation decisions.

coverage: All 32 pages: main sections 1–8, limitations; Appendices A.1–A.12, generation/filtering prompts and examples. Figure 4/5 performance plots visually inspected; tables and pipeline figures fully read.
problem: Synthetic SQL training data can be structurally simple, linguistically repetitive or incorrectly aligned, while discarding every ambiguous question removes useful alternative-interpretation supervision.
method: FALCON interleaves persona and reserved-word seeding, generates executable SQL then candidate questions, and combines a learned alignment filter with prompt-based screening. An Ambrosia-trained ambiguity scorer triggers generation and validation of a second interpretation. Implemented queries use SQLite.
evaluation: Generation/filtering ablations, small human-rated samples and Qwen 1.5B/3B fine-tuning compare synthetic, Spider and mixed data. The ambiguity pipeline is audited on 100 examples. Downstream measures include raw string match, string similarity and result-overlap scores, with difficulty-stratified plots.
findings: The ambiguity audit reports 94% accuracy but only 28.6% recall and 66.7% precision. Synthetic-only training improves harder-query slices while losing aggregate Spider performance; the 3B result-overlap score is 0.32 versus 0.42 for Spider training. Mixing 5% Spider restores much of string-match performance.
limitations: High specificity does not imply complete ambiguity coverage. Complexity and linguistic richness are weighted proxies, and partial result overlap is not semantic correctness. Mixed-model execution results are absent. The 1.5B setup supplies gold-query tables, making it different from unrestricted schema selection. Cost savings are estimated from assumed throughput and prices. Human subsets are described as disjoint, leaving inter-rater reliability unclear.
relevance: A relevant synthesis approach for retaining some semantic alternatives in training data, with evidence for controlled complexity coverage rather than demonstrated clarification or abstention capability.

claims.disposition: Describe as a scenario estimate, not measured benchmark cost.

coverage: All 27 public PDF pages: main sections 1–5; limitations; Appendices A–L including discovery protocol, published fact-sheet description, scoring audit, open-decision case study, delivery setup, repeat-run failures, resource reconciliation and complete displayed prompts. problem: An enterprise SQL system must satisfy requirements that customers initially leave vague, and benchmark accuracy alone may miss deployment constraints.
method: A fact-sheet-grounded customer simulator supports discovery of 17 known requirements while preserving six explicitly unknown decisions. Agents submit requirements and then use autonomous or separated planning/execution workflows to post-train and profile an Oracle-dialect SQL model under stated resource limits.
evaluation: Discovery covers 15 models, three disclosure levels and ten runs per condition. Delivery compares eight model/workflow configurations, with a separate harness comparison and repeated GPT-6.1 runs. Acceptance combines Spider-dev accuracy, compilation failures on 100 production questions and CPU p90 latency; BIRD is report-only.
findings: Automatic judgments report roughly 60% pooled recovery and over 80% for leading discovery models. Two of eight selected delivery results pass all three gates. Repeated GPT-6.1 trials complete training in three of six runs and pass once, illustrating that completion and acceptance differ.
limitations: This is one enterprise engagement with simulated customers and a historical human reference. Discovery label agreement is 70.6% for recovery on only 51 audited fact instances. Production questions lack reference SQL, so compilation does not measure their semantic accuracy. The 25% figure describes selected configuration results, not a broad success-rate estimate; open measurement choices, differing reasoning budgets and reported resource-allocation deviations constrain causal comparison.
relevance: Extends clarification research from individual SQL requests to deployment requirements and their handoff, highlighting unresolved decisions, fact loss and the gap between benchmark quality and operational acceptance.

coverage: Sections 1-8 and Appendix 9.1-9.6, Algorithms 1-3, Tables 1-8, Figures 1-9/captions and all prompt examples.
problem: Identify fully supported, partially supported and out-of-scope requests while diversifying NL2SQL training language without losing entities.
method: Combines schema-conditioned entity extraction, learned column-matching types, optional entity search and entity-preserving paraphrase generation. Scope labels rely on identified-column presence; paraphrasing is offline augmentation.

relevance: Explicit partial answerability is valuable, but component accuracy and successful interactive resolution must remain distinct.

coverage: All 37 pages: sections 1–6, references and Appendices A–K, including all prompts, reward equations, ablations, human-study details and complete example outputs; reasoning-length figure visually inspected.
problem: Models often commit to one plausible interpretation or produce opaque alternatives, even when a question admits several valid answers.
method: IntentRL applies DAPO to generate up to five interpretation–answer pairs in one response. Ambiguous training examples receive answer-set recall reward; unambiguous examples receive precision reward. Three-to-one oversampling of ambiguous cases counteracts training collapse toward one answer.
evaluation: The main Qwen3-4B model is tested on Abg-CoQA and AMBROSIA, with AMBROSIA-to-AmbiQT transfer, other model families, reward/data-format ablations and a simulated clarification pipeline. Human raters assess interpretation–answer compatibility on 30 ambiguous examples per main dataset.
findings: On AMBROSIA, reported full coverage rises from 58.8% for SFT to 74.1%; on AmbiQT it reaches 49.1%. Balancing is important, while answer-only RL remains competitive. SQL precision stays imperfect, and conversational QA frequently over-generates alternatives.
limitations: Human alignment judgments explicitly allow incorrect answers and do not establish truth, user preference or safer decisions. The five-answer limit excludes large interpretation spaces; execution matching remains instance-dependent. Clarification comparisons use simulated users and untrained clarification stages. One generation does not imply lower token cost, and precision is not directly rewarded on ambiguous examples.
relevance: Offers a trainable coverage-versus-restraint baseline and structured alternatives for clarification interfaces, with a clear distinction between answer coverage, explanation alignment and actual user-intent resolution.

claims.disposition: Attribute gains to training objective and sampling, not format alone.

coverage: All 22 pages: main sections 1–4 and limitations; Appendices A–D, operator contracts, all five prompt templates, split/implementation descriptions, ablations, sensitivity, convergence and efficiency tables.
problem: User questions omit domain conventions such as bridge joins, derived metrics and default filters, while historical question–SQL pairs may already encode them.
method: KODE aligns language-evidence and SQL graphs, extracts unmatched regions into five reusable template families, and retrieves rules before exemplars. A critic localizes conflicts for bounded rewriting. Optional backfill promotes queries with execution consensus and no detected residual conflict, with versioning and conflict rollback.
evaluation: Controlled ScienceBenchmark comparisons test in-domain reuse; BIRD/Spider schema-disjoint experiments transfer delexicalized templates. A separate BIRD-Dev-Domain split uses 460 history examples and 1,074 test queries with human evidence withheld. Ablations isolate knowledge types; five sequential batches assess deployment accumulation with frozen within-batch memory.
findings: Reported ScienceBenchmark average execution accuracy improves by 11.1 points over the strongest controlled comparator; abstract transfer gains are smaller, 2.0–3.2 points. Automatic backfill reaches 92.1% execution-based promotion precision at 47.6% coverage and improves later batches relative to frozen empty memory.
limitations: Historical conventions can encode systematic mistakes or preferences that do not match a new user. Graph well-formedness and execution consensus cannot establish semantic correctness. The sequential experiment uses one fixed shuffled order and measures promotion by execution, not human intent. Latency excludes mining and ongoing audits; schema drift, adversarial logs and long-lived memory were not evaluated.
relevance: A concrete alternative to user clarification when trusted domain history supplies missing context, while exposing the unresolved need to decide when historical defaults are insufficient or unsafe to reuse.

claims.claim: Critic acceptance certifies semantic correctness.
claims.evidence: The operator-contract appendix explicitly limits checks to graph well-formedness; promotion relies on six of eight execution-equivalent candidates and no detected conflicts.
claims.disposition: Treat as heuristic filtering, not semantic proof or calibrated correctness.
