claims.disposition: Restrict transfer claims to abstract templates.

claims.disposition: Qualify as controlled evidence of filtered accumulation with residual errors.

coverage: All 13 pages: sections 1–7, agent-development process, data-generator/attack strategies, normalization/comparison rules, all eight result tables and references.
problem: A single database can conceal semantic SQL errors; targeted test data can expose discrepancies missed by ordinary execution matching.
method: Agent-assisted development produces heuristic baseline-data generation and mutation-specific attack strategies, with occasional SMT use, schema-consistency repair and optional cross-checking pools. EX+ normalizes nondeterminism and compares successful query executions.
evaluation: A sanitized 36,042-pair suite compares refutation counts and tool runtime, with common-support and no-ordering subsets. Some benchmark failures informed implementation. Unseen checks include LargeJoin/TPC-H and ten BEAVER queries from one schema; the BEAVER outcome is non-empty-data generation, not pair refutation.
findings: LASSO and pairwise cross-checking refute more pairs overall under the reported protocol. Broader cross-instance pooling yields smaller incremental gains at higher cost. The most effective attacks target table/join coverage, boundaries, grouping and null behavior.
limitations: Survival is not proof of equivalence. Sanitization, dialect conversion, ordering/type policies and supported features affect comparisons. Reported tool times exclude external dataset loading and query execution. Human oversight remained necessary to catch shortcuts; broad unseen-workload generalization is not established.
relevance: A practical counterexample generator and test-development study, not an NL-to-SQL accuracy metric or formal equivalence certifier.

coverage: All eighteen PDF pages, Sections 1-5, limitations/ethics and Appendices A-E; equations, tables, algorithms and translated screenshot examples covered.
problem: Refusal based on generated text or repeated SQL samples can be costly and can happen after questionable SQL has already been produced.
method: A frozen local LLM provides intermediate activations to a supervised Tri-Residual Gated Encoder. A thresholded answerability score controls SQL generation. The probe adds attention, feed-forward and SwiGLU residual branches; its development-set selection is deployment-specific.
evaluation: Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B are evaluated on four separately trained dataset groups, including ambiguity, TriageSQL, reading comprehension and a nonpublic enterprise set. Each dataset has a sampled 300-example test set; architecture and layer ablations use TriageSQL.
findings: Average F1 is reported as 88.5% and 88.8%. TRGE improves over the tested pooled/linear and latent baselines, but not every model-dataset cell is best. Probe-only latency is a few milliseconds; it excludes the backbone forward pass.
limitations: White-box activations and new-domain supervised adaptation are required. The semantic-entropy SQL baseline uses syntactic agreement. Appendix algorithms for additional hallucination detection and domain-specific probes are explicitly outside the main results. Safe refusal labels do not certify correctness of admitted SQL.
relevance: Supports efficient pre-generation screening, with a clear boundary between answerability prediction and semantic verification.

claims.disposition: Report supervised adaptation across settings, not zero-shot transfer.

claims.disposition: Keep hardware and measurement boundaries; do not present probe latency as end-to-end latency.

claims.disposition: No downstream SQL-correctness guarantee is established.

coverage: All 15 pages: main sections 1–5; Appendices A–H, error study, pipeline/agent procedures, single-database adaptations, complete AmbiDB construction and filtering, efficiency and limitations. Figure 2–3 plots visually inspected.
problem: A SQL system given many databases may retrieve incomplete schemas, select irrelevant databases, or lose necessary tables and columns inside the correct database.
method: LinkAlign uses iterative query rewriting to improve retrieval, filters candidate databases, then extracts relevant schema items. Each stage has a cheaper single-prompt implementation and a multi-agent alternative. AmbiDB expands Spider with overlapping schemas and rewrites questions while retaining clues intended to identify one target database.
evaluation: Schema-linking experiments on Spider, BIRD and AmbiDB measure target-database location, exact schema recovery and recall. Single-database tests assess grounding; SQL generation is evaluated on Spider/BIRD and Spider 2.0-lite. Ablations remove retrieval rewriting and filtering, and a 50-example sample measures end-to-end runtime.
findings: The agent implementation improves schema exact match across the reported datasets, while retrieval and precision/recall trade-offs vary. On AmbiDB, pipeline database-location accuracy exceeds the agent variant, and competing methods attain higher recall. The paper reports a historical 33.09% Spider 2.0-lite result with DeepSeek-R1.
limitations: This is automatic schema selection, not user-intent clarification or abstention. AmbiDB is synthetic and deliberately preserves disambiguating clues; its public release availability is a separate artifact question. Strongest performance claims do not hold for every metric, and headline SQL comparisons use differing backbones. Extra agent reasoning increases measured runtime.
relevance: An adjacent benchmark for retrieval ambiguity in large schema pools, useful for separating failure to find the intended database from genuine missing information that requires asking the user.

claims.claim: AmbiDB represents inherently unresolved user-intent ambiguity.
claims.evidence: Construction adds overlapping schemas but deliberately incorporates subtle clues to determine the target database and avoid complete confusion.
claims.disposition: Scope to synthetic schema-selection difficulty with an intended target.

claims.claim: LinkAlign outperforms every baseline on every schema metric.
claims.evidence: Table 2 gives AmbiDB agent recall 56.9 versus RSL-SQL 59.6; Table 3 gives AmbiDB recall 85.8 versus MCS-SQL 88.5 and RSL-SQL 88.3.
claims.disposition: Retain exact-match improvements but qualify blanket superiority.

claims.evidence: The paper explicitly dates its first-place statement to submission and uses different model backbones across compared entries.
claims.disposition: Report as historical paper result, not current or controlled superiority.

coverage: Proceedings pp. 5447-5458, Sections 1-6, Tables 1-5 and figure captions; arXiv supplementary pp. 13-14, Appendices A-C and Tables 6-12. Rendered Table 5 inspected.
problem: Interactive semantic parsing needs reusable components for deciding when to seek user help and incorporating that feedback during generation.
method: Maintains a partial parse, flags uncertain components using probability or Monte Carlo dropout, asks template-based yes/no questions, and bans rejected alternatives in the base parser. Candidate attempts are capped; rejecting every alternative restores the original prediction.
evaluation: SQLNet and SQLova on WikiSQL and SyntaxSQLNet on Spider; ground-truth-driven simulation plus three graduate evaluators per sampled example. The study reports query matching, execution accuracy and question counts; its human sample is 100 examples per base parser.
findings: Selective interaction improves simulated accuracy with fewer questions than exhaustive querying. Human gains are smaller; SQLova execution accuracy is 0.880 versus 0.890 without interaction, despite a slight exact-match gain. Showing table content and gold SQL raises its result to 0.937.
limitations: Human feedback depends on understanding benchmark intent. The full-information condition exposes gold SQL and is not ordinary deployment. Error correction is bounded by the parser’s candidate set and earlier decisions; no request-unanswerability guarantee is provided.
relevance: Foundational architecture and evidence that simulator gains and oracle-informed users can overstate practical clarification benefits.

claims.claim: Human interaction improves performance in all settings.
claims.evidence: Table 5 shows SQLova exact match 0.830 to 0.837 but execution accuracy 0.890 to 0.880; full-information execution is 0.937.
claims.disposition: Qualify by metric and information access; not a uniform human improvement.

claims.evidence: SyntaxSQLNet is wrapped with expanded NLG rules; accuracy remains 0.290 at 2.905 questions in the displayed setting.
claims.disposition: Supported for the tested parser integration, not unrestricted generalization.

coverage: All 10 actual PDF pages, sections I–VII, appendices A–C, tables I–VIII; rendered question-distribution and performance figures inspected. PDF text contained spurious form-feed glyphs, repaired by per-page extraction.
problem: Conversation turns require different behavior for answerable, ambiguous, unsupported and improper requests.
method: MMSQL combines refined CoSQL records with Gemini-generated QDA-SQL dialogues. A schema selector, question detector, decomposer and SQL refiner choose responses and generate/repair candidate queries.
evaluation: Eight base LLMs and three multi-agent variants are evaluated on a curated 149-dialogue test. SQL metrics and type classification are separate; TDEX scores SQL execution for answerable/ambiguous turns but type matching for other turns. GPT-4o-mini judges response quality, with a 100-sample human comparison.
findings: The multi-agent configuration improves the reported aggregate scores, particularly for weaker baselines. Ambiguity classification and SQL after ambiguous requests remain challenging. Removing the detector hurts several measures; removing the refiner does not reduce every metric.
limitations: This evaluates curated/generated conversation records rather than uncontrolled real-user interaction. Class frequencies differ sharply between training and test. Prose reverses some Table V unanswerable/ambiguous precision-recall values, and Figure 3 execution numbers coincide with Table III exact-match values; avoid unqualified numeric comparisons.
relevance: A mixed-question routing benchmark; its hybrid TDEX and model-judged response quality need explicit interpretation.

coverage: All eleven PDF pages, Sections 1-8, limitations and Appendix A; Tables 1-6 and all figure descriptions/examples covered.
problem: Read-only conversational SQL benchmarks miss dialogue-driven changes to database contents and schema.
method: GPT-4 extends CoSQL-derived interactions with SELECT and mutation/schema operations. Human correction removes errors and adds contextual dependencies. The prompt baseline supplies dialogue history and optional executor feedback for self-refinement.
evaluation: The final corpus contains 783 dialogues and 9,257 turns over 166 databases. Llama tuning uses 662 dialogues, with 121 reserved for testing. Metrics include SELECT execution accuracy, heuristic name-mapped context-aware matching and database-state matching for mutations.
findings: History and refinement improve several GPT-4 results, including SELECT execution accuracy, but gains are not uniform across operations or weaker models. Long dialogue and schema changes remain difficult.
limitations: The dialogue corpus is synthesized and manually refined rather than sampled live user interaction. Appendix A uses GPT-3.5 to extract SQL from Llama outputs, so those results include postprocessing assistance. Fuzzy identifier matching and instance-state comparisons do not establish unrestricted semantic equivalence. Explicit clarification and unanswerability policies are not evaluated.
relevance: Useful for testing state tracking and error propagation in database agents, separately from recognizing ambiguity.

claims.claim: Self-refinement generally improves performance.

coverage: All 12 PDF pages: Sections 1-10, definitions, query-tree algorithm, SQL translation examples and Figures 1-13 with captions; no appended supplement.
problem: Let non-SQL users verify interpretations of complex database requests rather than trust opaque answer values.
method: Maps dependency-tree nodes to schema/data, proposes alternative query trees, inserts inferred implicit nodes under user control and translates the selected tree to SQL. Changing an earlier choice recomputes dependent later interpretations.
evaluation: A 14-participant within-subject study on Microsoft Academic Search compares interactive NaLIR, noninteractive NaLIR and website navigation. Tasks are conveyed in Chinese and written as English queries; condition order is fixed.
findings: Interactive users solve 88/98 tasks versus 64/98 without interaction and 56/98 through the website. Four incorrect outputs are still accepted. Candidate-tree coverage limits difficult requests.
limitations: Evidence covers one domain and a small bilingual sample; fixed ordering permits learning effects. Reported time measures only successful tasks. Heuristic implicit-node insertion and top-five interpretations do not guarantee intent correctness.
relevance: Establishes interpretation feedback and dependency-aware reprocessing as practical design ideas, while showing residual user verification failures.

claims.claim: The system is broadly reliable and usable.
claims.evidence: The single-domain study supports improved task completion, but four wrong answers were accepted and difficult query trees were missing from menus.
claims.disposition: Bound to the tested users/tasks; not universal reliability.

claims.claim: Interaction time remains practical.
claims.evidence: The timing excludes unsuccessful tasks and a three-minute timeout applies.
claims.disposition: Successful-task timing, not full workload latency.

coverage: All 12 PDF pages: Sections 1-9, Algorithm 1, Tables 1-6, Figures 1-5 with captions and references. No appended supplement in this version.
problem: Correct an erroneous SQL parse from free-form feedback grounded in the original question, schema and query explanation.
method: Represents changes as clause-level add/remove operations and predicts linearized edits using BERT, relation-aware encoding and a Transformer decoder. Synthetic mutation-feedback pairs pretrain the model before SPLASH fine-tuning.
evaluation: One supplied feedback turn on SPLASH and additional EditSQL, TaBERT and RAT-SQL errors. Exact-set-match correction is accompanied by relative edit reduction; the representation discards condition values and restricts subquery structure.
findings: Correction accuracy rises from 25.16% to 41.17%; errors decrease for 72.41% of examples but increase for 16.93%. End-to-end gains shrink as the base parser improves, from 20.3 points for Seq2Struct to 4.3 for RAT-SQL.
limitations: Recorded one-turn corrections do not establish multi-turn convergence. Longer explanations and irrelevant extra edits remain failure modes; edit-distance improvement is a structural proxy rather than complete semantic validation.
relevance: A useful feedback-integration baseline, with explicit evidence that editing can damage previously correct query components.

claims.claim: The model improves correction by 16%.
claims.evidence: Table 2 compares 41.17% with 25.16%, a 16.01-percentage-point gain.
claims.disposition: Use percentage points and preserve the one-turn protocol.

claims.claim: Progress implies faster convergence.
claims.evidence: Progress measures relative edit reduction after one response; 16.93% of examples gain errors.
claims.disposition: Partial repair evidence, not observed multi-turn convergence or preservation guarantee.

coverage: All twelve PDF pages, Sections 1-7 and Appendices A-B, 31-subtype taxonomy, annotation protocol, all result tables and worked SQL cases.
problem: Executable SQL can be wrong relative to a natural-language request, and detecting the error class is harder than judging a query as wrong.
method: The authors screen BIRD reference questions/SQL, generate candidates with RESDSQL, CodeS and CHESS, deduplicate SQL, then annotate incorrect queries using a nine-category/31-subtype taxonomy. Two SQL experts label types, with third-expert adjudication.
evaluation: The 2,018 instances comprise 1,019 labeled correct and 999 incorrect candidates. Six LLMs perform binary correctness and multi-label type detection. Correctness labeling primarily compares execution results with screened reference SQL; subtype evaluation uses the fraction of true instances whose label is found.
findings: Binary accuracy is around three quarters while type identification is substantially weaker. The paper also reports manually validated candidate reference errors in Spider and BIRD.
limitations: The stated semantic task includes errors hidden by current-instance agreement, but result-based labels can miss those cases. Type-Specific Accuracy is recall-like and does not itself penalize extra predicted types. Generator mix, selected BIRD references and expert labeling conventions limit transfer.
relevance: A benchmark for candidate-SQL verifiers and error explanations, separate from deciding whether the original request is answerable.

claims.claim: Type-Specific Accuracy is classification accuracy.
claims.evidence: The Section 5.3 formula divides correctly found type labels by all instances truly containing that type, without a false-positive denominator.
claims.disposition: Describe as per-type recall-like coverage, not ordinary overall accuracy.

claims.claim: Correct labels establish universal semantic correctness.
claims.evidence: Section 2 includes current-instance accidental agreement as an error, but Section 4.2 assigns correctness primarily through execution-result matching.
claims.disposition: Retain the instance/reference-bound labeling limitation.

coverage: All nine PDF pages: Sections 1–4, conclusions and limitations, Algorithm 1, Tables 1–2, the AST example, references and all 13 Appendix A examples. Table 1 visually inspected.
problem: Locate suspect components in generated SQL instead of assigning one confidence score to the entire query.
method: A reference-AST alignment heuristic normalizes aliases and operator symmetry, suppresses blame on containers and globally rescues matching nodes. A LightGBM classifier uses 72 structural, lexical and schema features without reference SQL at inference.
evaluation: OmniSQL-7B generates BIRD development candidates and 67,901 SynSQL candidates from 453 databases. Experiments compare query splits within databases, three held-out BIRD databases, and SynSQL-to-BIRD transfer using node-level ROC-AUC against heuristic labels.
findings: Overall ROC-AUC is 76.51% in-database, 69.46% across BIRD databases and 66.47% after SynSQL training. Aggregate discrimination exceeds mean token log-probabilities, but not every node type improves; Table nodes are slightly worse in the first experiment.
limitations: Labels encode a comparison convention rather than full natural-language correctness. Missing predicates or other omitted clauses are intentionally unlabelled. Thirteen prototyping cases are not an independent label-quality audit. Only one SQL generator is evaluated, and ROC-AUC does not establish calibrated probabilities or useful downstream abstention.
relevance: A localized error-confidence baseline for verification and targeted review; direct ambiguity detection, clarification, repair effectiveness and selective-risk control remain untested.

claims.claim: The reported uncertainty probabilities are empirically calibrated.
claims.evidence: Section 1 interprets uncertainty as calibrated probability, while Section 4 and both result tables report ROC-AUC without calibration-error, reliability-diagram or proper-scoring evaluation.
claims.disposition: Support error ranking, not demonstrated probability calibration.

claims.claim: No erroneous generated nodes means a complete correct query.
claims.evidence: Remark 2 excludes omissions, and Appendix A Example 6 gives no incorrect nodes when ORDER BY is absent from the generated query.
claims.disposition: Node labels do not assess query completeness or general semantic correctness.

claims.claim: The headline 27.44% gain is a relative improvement across all settings.
claims.evidence: Table 1 aggregate AUC values are 76.51% and 49.07%, a 27.44-percentage-point difference in the in-database experiment; Table 2 has different cross-database/transfer values.
claims.disposition: Use percentage points and the specific evaluation condition.

coverage: All 22 pages, main sections 1–6 and Limitations; Appendices A–D with construction, paraphrase audit, simulator mechanics, statistics, supplementary/ablation experiments, algorithms and all displayed prompts.
problem: Queries may omit their intended attribute, table scope or entity condition, making open-corpus table retrieval and SQL generation fail before conventional parsing can succeed.
method: ODUTQA-MDC perturbs RETQA templates and entity values to create single and mixed SELECT/FROM/WHERE underspecification. A simulator reveals dictionary-held corrections only after the system predicts the required detection label. MAIC-TQA combines a fine-tuned intent/slot model, scope validation, table retrieval and SQL execution with bounded clarification loops.
evaluation: The Chinese real-estate collection contains 209 tables and 25,105 QA pairs with a 6:2:2 split. Five LLM backbones compare clarification-enabled MAIC-TQA against clarification-free SLUTQA. Measures separate detection, table retrieval, SQL executability and exact execution-result match; ablations remove each clarification stage.
findings: Clarification improves retrieval and execution accuracy in the reported setup. For Qwen3 32B, fixed clarification raises execution accuracy from 24.20% to 57.44%; dynamic paraphrasing changes outcomes differently across models. Scope and condition clarification account for the largest ablation losses.
limitations: The task is deliberately filtered toward recoverable, answerable targets and excludes complex aggregation and broad linguistic ambiguity. Its simulator rewards exact label detection with privileged target information; natural paraphrasing does not test human goal changes or refusal. MAIC’s BERT is fine-tuned on the new dataset while baseline BERT is loaded from its original release. Cross-domain generalization is proposed, not demonstrated.
relevance: A useful benchmark for coupling missing-information detection with table retrieval and clarification, provided its controlled correction protocol is distinguished from general answerability assessment.

claims.claim: The dataset directly tests unrecoverable unanswerability.
claims.evidence: Generation filters unsuitable cases for an answerable QA benchmark; the underlying target SQL remains unchanged and clarification dictionaries contain the correct values.
claims.disposition: Scope to recoverable underspecification and error correction.

claims.claim: Dynamic feedback is unconstrained natural user interaction.
claims.evidence: Corrections are revealed only after predicted labels match gold; dynamic mode paraphrases canonical facts with keyword checks and deterministic fallback.
claims.disposition: Describe label-gated, fact-preserving simulated interaction.

claims.claim: The experiment establishes cross-domain generality.
claims.evidence: All tables come from property, real-estate finance and land auctions, and the limitations explicitly leave other vertical industries to generalization.
claims.disposition: Limit empirical scope to the reported real-estate setting.

version: Findings of IJCNLP-AACL 2026 proceedings, pp. 3979–4002, November 6–10, 2026; 24-page published version
coverage: All 24 PDF pages: Sections 1–8, Tables 1–7, Algorithms 1–2, and complete Appendices A–D covering preprocessing, operator definitions, optimization, batching, experimental settings, extended results, error analysis and every supplied prompt. Result/error/sensitivity plots in Figures 3–15 visually inspected; Figures 1–2 captions and extracted architecture text read. The shorter arXiv version was checked for identity only, not treated as the reviewed full-text version.

additional_sources.label: Official implementation inspected at a fixed revision

problem: Queries over hybrid tables may require attributes hidden in text, while vague language admits several schema mappings or computational interpretations.
method: The system prunes and profiles schemas, constructs query-aware data previews, and generates alternative operator DAGs. Relational steps execute through SQL; semantic extraction, filtering, joining and aggregation use LLMs. Optimization and batching reduce costs, then a judge or semantic vote selects one candidate answer.
evaluation: RepairTQA supplies paired structured and textual representations; five additional table-QA benchmarks test transfer. Evaluation uses 100 examples per dataset/subset, except 50 for multi-table long. Reference-based LLM scoring measures answer correctness; reference-free candidate selection and oracle ACC@6 are reported separately.
findings: Diversification outperforms naive plan sampling in the displayed ablations, and optimization lowers token cost without changing those accuracy scores. The main RepairTQA comparison reports higher selected-answer accuracy, but gains do not hold against every baseline on every extended benchmark.
limitations: No user clarification, refusal policy or all-interpretation coverage is evaluated. Model-based answer scoring can err, and preprocessing may discard information. Confidence intervals use aggregate accuracies and nominal sample sizes rather than repeated-run variation. K/batch-size accuracy curves use oracle ACC@K. Token measurements do not establish end-to-end latency or semantic preservation guarantees.
relevance: An adjacent implementation direction for recovering missing structure and exploring alternative groundings before committing to an answer, with user-intent validation still unresolved.

claims.claim: ACC@6 is deployable single-answer accuracy.
claims.evidence: It counts success when any of six candidates matches the reference. A separate LLM selects the deployed answer without reference access.
claims.locator: Section 4 Settings, PDF p.6; Figure 3; Appendix C.2
claims.disposition: Keep oracle candidate coverage separate from selected-answer performance.

claims.claim: Plan diversification resolves the user’s ambiguity.
claims.evidence: Section 3.2 generates alternative schema mappings and vague-intent criteria; Section 3.3 consolidates outputs automatically. Human plan auditing is future work.
claims.locator: Sections 3.2–3.3; Section 7; Appendix D consolidation prompts
claims.disposition: It explores and selects possible groundings, without confirming the intended reading or measuring clarification success.

claims.claim: Accuracy improvements are universal across extended benchmarks.
claims.evidence: Figure 4 shows Direct-LLM above the selected-answer OmniTQA result on FeTaQA and TAT-QA; oracle ACC@6 is higher than the selected-answer result.
claims.disposition: Retain dataset- and consolidation-specific comparisons.

coverage: All 34 pages: sections 1–9, references, Appendices A–H, every audit/robustness table, registration history and artifact disclosure; key risk, alignment and frontier plots visually inspected.
problem: Execution-based calibration labels and the database used to cluster candidates can jointly determine an abstention system’s reported risk, without reliably measuring semantic correctness.
method: A two-by-two intervention crosses shipped-database versus multi-instance partitions with calibration labels, holding sampled candidates and answer selection fixed. The study audits rejected outputs with AI and separately obtains blinded expert labels for reference defects and both accepted/rejected outputs.
evaluation: Four SQL-specialist checkpoints, three seeds and 508 Spider-Realistic questions are evaluated with repeated question splits and schema-disjoint stress tests. Expert answer labels cover two checkpoints at one seed. The paper distinguishes preregistered panel outcomes from later score comparisons, relabeling and robustness analyses.
findings: Suite labels raise measured risk by 2.73–10.23 points, but expert judgments show that neither oracle uniformly measures semantic risk. Most risk reduction comes from changing which questions receive answers. Oracle-aligned score advantages shrink or persist depending on the checkpoint under independent labels.
limitations: The certified loss is marginal wrong-answer probability, not error conditional on answering; database splits lack the exchangeability guarantee. The benchmark and endpoint were selected during exploration before fresh panel generation. AI census categories are not all human-validated, and expert coverage is limited. Archived code/results are available, but complete experiment reproduction was not performed.
relevance: Directly motivates reporting calibration/evaluation oracles, answer rates, loss definitions and independent semantic audits alongside abstention guarantees, rather than equating stricter execution labels with truth.

claims.claim: The 0.10 certificate controls error among answered questions and unseen databases.
claims.evidence: Abstention receives zero loss; Section 3.1 explicitly distinguishes marginal from selective risk and calls database splits non-exchangeable stress tests.
claims.disposition: Correct guarantee scope.

claims.claim: All five census labels and all checkpoint risks are independently expert-validated.
claims.evidence: Reference audit tests one question-level label; answer audit covers two checkpoints at seed 101. Other census labels remain AI-only.
claims.disposition: Qualify audit coverage.

claims.claim: No public study artifacts exist.
claims.evidence: Paper Appendix F links official repository; public README now lists expanded released outputs, and c4_recompute.py plus c4_panel_summary.json were retrieved successfully. This is newer than the PDF statement that study data were not public.
claims.disposition: Update code and verified-results availability; no reproduction claim.

coverage: All thirteen PDF pages, Sections 1-7, Definitions 1-6, symbolic/hybrid algorithms, coverage constraints, experimental tables and figure descriptions; no appendices.
problem: Fixed databases and local SQL mutations miss inequivalence caused by operator interactions, ties, multiplicity and grouping.
method: ParSEval expresses logical-plan operator behaviors as coverage constraints, then solves for small databases. A hybrid approach speculatively assigns concrete values to reduce symbolic expressions, with fallback solving. Relaxed coverage avoids enumerating every constraint combination.
evaluation: Four corpora include BIRD/Spider model predictions and human-written LeetCode/literature pairs. Comparisons use a 360-second timeout. Pair-aware evaluation generates tests from both queries; a separate experiment precomputes suites from gold queries alone.
findings: The hybrid implementation improves supported-query coverage and counterexample discovery against the evaluated open-source baselines. A manual BIRD inequivalence audit reports 91.01% recall. Gold-only suites are smaller and faster than original databases but still admit 41 false positives in the reported experiment.
limitations: NULL multiplicities, special functions and unseen extra joins can evade generated tests. Supported/unknown outcomes and timeouts affect comparisons; some competing provers were excluded for missing released foreign-key support. Complete branch coverage is not a proof of unrestricted query equivalence or reference-intent validity.
relevance: Offers richer execution evidence and concrete counterexamples for evaluating SQL verifiers and candidate generation.

claims.claim: Plan coverage ensures semantic equivalence.
claims.evidence: Definition 1 distinguishes test-suite equivalence from semantic equivalence; Sections 5.3/5.5 document remaining false positives.
claims.disposition: Only a distinguishing instance proves inequivalence; passing the finite suite remains incomplete.

claims.claim: The same recall applies to reusable gold-only suites.
claims.evidence: Main pair evaluation generates tests from both queries; Section 5.5 uses only gold queries and lists extra-join misses.
claims.disposition: Keep candidate-aware and precomputed-suite protocols separate.

coverage: All 33 PDF pages: Sections 1-6, limitations, Appendices A-I, algorithms, sufficiency extraction, all six detailed SQL/trajectory case studies, robustness controls and PRACTIQ comparison. Visually checked PDF pages 30 and 32 for cost and efficiency figures.
problem: Interactive SQL agents can spend scarce environment calls generating queries before obtaining necessary schema, business rules or user intent.
method: PASCAL uses training-free source-aware acquisition gates, schema injection, typed knowledge retrieval, informed clarification, bounded retries and follow-up state carry. A gold-derived coverage score diagnoses missing evidence after execution; it is not a runtime oracle.
evaluation: A local Qwen3.6-35B backbone is evaluated on BIRD-Interact Lite/Full, with additive ablations, schema-matched controls and 100-task simulator, budget and retry sensitivity experiments. PRACTIQ evaluation uses a 1,069-task subset and an explicit abstention path.
findings: The paper reports 51.0% first-phase and 37.0% cumulative two-phase success on Lite, with larger gains on knowledge-intensive queries. Controls support a benefit beyond initial schema access; delayed clarification still creates regressions. Three subset runs yield 54, 54 and 53 percent first-phase success.
limitations: Coverage is partly constructed from submitted SQL mentions and gold annotations, not independent semantic understanding. Cost totals and detailed trajectories conflict with stated budgets, and value-diff case studies are not reconciled with the no-value-diff result setting. PRACTIQ abstention and prior post-clarification SQL scores require protocol qualification.
relevance: Offers concrete acquisition-control mechanisms and diagnostics; numerical efficiency and leaderboard-equivalence claims need clarification before reuse.

claims.claim: The sufficiency score independently verifies evidence acquisition.
claims.evidence: Appendix D counts tables/columns from SQL arguments and intent via token overlap, uses gold sets, and explicitly acknowledges partly construction-induced association.
claims.disposition: Describe a post-hoc proxy, not a proof or independent causal test.

claims.claim: Reported tool counts reconcile with the stated coin budget.
claims.evidence: Table 38 charges 3 coins per submission; Appendix I.4 reports 5.7 submissions but only 12.6 total coins/task. Submissions alone imply 17.1 coins. Table 37 also lists 31 failed submissions before success against a stated 30-coin budget.
claims.locator: Table 37, Table 38; Appendix G.3; Appendix I.4
claims.disposition: Flag reporting inconsistency; do not publish exact efficiency or equal-budget superiority as established.

claims.claim: The diagnostic cases use the stated no-value-diff condition.
claims.evidence: Appendix G.1 says all numbers use NVD, while F.2 and F.4 show access to expected numeric outputs and use value-diff feedback to recover formulas.
claims.disposition: Keep case evidence and aggregate NVD claims distinct pending reconciliation.

version: AACL-IJCNLP 2026 proceedings, pages 5377–5391; complete 15-page publisher PDF.
coverage: All 15 PDF pages: Sections 1–8, limitations, references and Appendices A–H; all prompts, decoding details, policy-construction rules and Tables 1–11. Figures 1–2 were visually inspected. Artifact source and license inspection was textual only.
problem: Database interfaces must refuse or adapt requests when the allowed use of a column depends on whether it is projected, filtered, joined or aggregated.
method: PCC-SQL tracks grammar roles and scope, masks disallowed column tokens and emits REFUSE when continuation is blocked, validation fails or syntax is unsupported. Four permission types distinguish public, condition-only, aggregate-only and hidden columns.
evaluation: Three open models are compared with prompting, retry, verification and rollback on Spider-CU, BIRD-CU and Spider-ACL. Synthetic policies use column-name rules and reference-query usage. Coverage measures compliant output; execution match is separately measured only on SQL-gold cases. Spider-ACL omits runtime execution checks.
findings: The paper reports zero policy violations in the tested decoder cells and high compliant-output coverage. These figures do not imply correct answers: weaker-model execution accuracy can decrease, and compliant alternatives on REFUSE-gold cases are not checked against intent-equivalent references.
limitations: Policy validity has only a 40-assignment author sanity check. Guarantees cover supported single-query column roles, excluding richer SQL, multi-query inference and broader privacy properties. Unsupported syntax or difficult planning can cause false refusal. Logits access is required, while token/call measurements omit wall-clock latency and masking overhead.
relevance: A concrete adjacent baseline for permission-dependent refusal and constrained answering. Its labels distinguish prohibited query uses from missing information, ambiguous intent or proof that no valid answer exists.

claims.claim: Coverage and Recovery Rate measure semantically correct answers or restored user intent.
claims.evidence: SafeSQL means policy compliance and executability, and Refuse-gold can receive any compliant alternative. Appendix G tests execution match only on SQL-gold; Appendix E omits runtime checks entirely for Spider-ACL.
claims.locator: Section 5.4; Section 6.3; Appendices C, E and G; Table 11
claims.disposition: Keep compliant-output coverage separate from semantic correctness, and state the Spider-ACL execution exception.

claims.claim: A REFUSE label establishes intrinsic unanswerability.
claims.evidence: Appendix C assigns REFUSE when the reference SQL violates the constructed policy. Appendix B also refuses unsupported grammar, out-of-scope references, failed validation or an empty allowed set; the limitations acknowledge refusal even when a safe alternative exists.
claims.disposition: Describe policy/decoder-relative refusal, not missing-fact impossibility or complete detection of all admissible answers.

claims.claim: Zero leakage establishes broad privacy protection with measured low latency.
claims.evidence: The guarantee is limited to supported single-query column-use compliance. The limitations exclude inference attacks, joint-distribution leakage and differential privacy, and explicitly say wall-clock latency and mask overhead were not measured.
claims.disposition: Qualify the guarantee's grammar and threat scope; report call/token cost rather than end-to-end latency.

coverage: All ten PDF pages: Sections 1-8, equations, Tables 1-3, Figures 1-6 and captions, modifier examples and references. No appended supplement in this version.
problem: Improve a black-box Text-to-SQL parser by resolving expressions it fails to align with the generated SQL.
method: Restates SQL through templates, aligns question and restatement tokens with a weakly trained BERT model, asks ranked multiple-choice questions, and rewrites the original question with POS-dependent rules. Database contents are not read.
evaluation: Five parsers on WikiSQL and Spider. Simulation filters options using reference SQL and searches up to 100 combinations. A separate 300-question Spider study involves 30 non-SQL-expert volunteers, three judgments per question.
findings: Human interaction raises IRNet and IRNet+BERT exact-match accuracy by 3.7 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively. Simulation reports larger gains. Rule-based rewriting outperforms direct token replacement in the tested IRNet setup.
limitations: The reference-assisted simulator is an idealized selection procedure. Candidate menus, supported SQL restatement grammar and modifier rules restrict generality; None preserves unchanged text but cannot ensure the intended option is offered.
relevance: Provides a black-box clarification interface and measured human/simulator gap, not a general answerability detector.

claims.claim: The approach improves arbitrary parsers with limited interaction.
claims.evidence: Five selected parsers improve, but simulation uses reference-filtered options and oracle outcome search.
claims.disposition: Supported for evaluated parsers and grammar; broad arbitrary-parser deployment remains untested.

claims.claim: Human interaction improves performance.
claims.evidence: Table 2 compares 49.0 to 52.7 and 60.7 to 62.2 on the same 300-question subset.
claims.disposition: Positive subset gains; separate from full development-set simulation.

coverage: All 22 pages: Sections 1-7, AI/reproducibility statements, Appendices A-D, Algorithms 1-2, case-study SQL, tables and complete method-specific prompts.
problem: Agents can identify useful clarification questions yet silently abandon them before generating SQL, producing apparently correct but weakly grounded answers.
method: Stores a ranked question pool outside conversational context, permits explicit additions/removals, routes questions through a pool tool, and blocks final submission while items remain. The generator, datasource tools and simulated-user backbone are held fixed across strategy variants.
evaluation: 171 BIRD-Lite and 225 BIRD-Full cases are selected because the same agent succeeds with all clarifications supplied; 297 Spider cases contain injected ambiguities. Claude-Opus-4.8 plays agent and simulator. Metrics distinguish execution, annotated-ambiguity coverage and cost.
findings: Pool enforcement improves annotated recall and grounded success over prompt-only planning while asking more questions. It does not maximize execution accuracy: on BIRD-Full, self-reflection scores 70.7% versus 67.1% for PlanPool.
limitations: Groundedness counts an ambiguity as addressed when a simulator maps a question to it, rather than verifying faithful incorporation of the answer. Solvability filtering conditions results on the chosen model; tool action costs are removed. Explicit dropping and incomplete initial plans prevent any guarantee that all real ambiguities are resolved.
relevance: A concrete persistent clarification-state mechanism with conditional simulator evidence and a distinct accounting-versus-resolution boundary.

claims.claim: PlanPool improves resolution groundedness.
claims.evidence: Table 2 improves annotated coverage, but Appendix B operationalizes addressed ambiguity through question mapping by the simulator encoder.
claims.disposition: Supported for the operational coverage metric, not verified interpretation uptake.

claims.claim: Results characterize general BIRD-Interact performance.
claims.evidence: Appendix A retains only 171/300 Lite and 225/600 Full cases solved after oracle clarification and drops implementation ambiguity categories.
claims.disposition: Conditional ambiguity-handling evaluation, not full-benchmark accuracy.

version: arXiv:2603.01795v1, 2 March 2026; arXiv records CHI 2026 acceptance and publisher DOI
coverage: All 17 pages: sections 1–12, pragmatic formalization/equations, algorithm evaluation, interface design, user-study methods/results, limitations and references; rendered algorithm, performance, interface and study-result figures/table inspected.
problem: Users cannot steer underspecified requests when an interface hides alternative SQL interpretations and the consequences of clarification.
method: The system samples up to 50 syntactically valid SQL candidates, groups execution-output similarities, extracts atomic/grouped decision variables and ranks them by expected information gain. Linked visual views allow filtering, comparison and undo over this fixed candidate pool.
evaluation: An AMBROSIA simulation uses gold-consistent clarification choices and tracks entropy/output similarity. A separate study involves 12 SQL-familiar participants and five small filmmaking-domain tasks, with think-aloud interaction and component/usability questionnaires.
findings: Clustering can reduce uncertainty in fewer idealized turns, and participants discover alternatives and use several repair workflows. Reported 84.4% task completion averages 180 subtasks and counts partial solutions as correct; seven participants missed their initial interpretation on at least one task.
limitations: The fixed generated pool can exclude the desired query. Execution similarity on one small database is approximate, not semantic equivalence. The interface requires SQL familiarity, and the user study does not establish benefits for nontechnical users or large databases. Changing or initially unclear intent is outside the controlled algorithm experiment.
relevance: An interaction-design and candidate-filtering contribution with explicit coverage limitations, rather than unrestricted natural-language intent recovery.

claims.claim: 84.4% means exact original-query success.
claims.evidence: Section 10.1 footnote counts partial outcomes across 180 subtasks; text reports 7/12 participants unable to find their initial interpretation for at least one task.
claims.disposition: Do not interpret the figure as exact original-intent SQL accuracy.

claims.claim: The interface is validated for SQL-naive end users.
claims.evidence: Section 9.1 requires basic SQL familiarity; section 11.2 describes it as a research tool and leaves nontechnical accessibility open.
claims.disposition: Scope human evidence to the recruited SQL-familiar sample.

coverage: All 35 pages: main sections 1–8, formal definitions/proofs, Algorithms 1–3, experimental tables and dialect analysis; Appendix A complete examples and repair prompts P1–P9.
problem: Execution-error feedback gives incomplete repair guidance, and a model may fix one SQL defect while deleting useful structure or reintroducing an earlier error.
method: Post-SQLFix canonicalizes SQL, diagnoses syntax, structural and schema/type violations, and constrains repair candidates with explicit edit contracts. A monitor accepts only transitions that reduce violation count, preserve protected components and avoid recurring resolved violations. A separate optional heuristic substitutes columns for empty-result predicates.
evaluation: Gen-SQL and TA-SQL are evaluated on BIRD, Spider and BIRD Mini-Dev under SQLite, MySQL and PostgreSQL, with six repair proposers. Full-pipeline integration includes upstream schema-linking checks; repair-only comparisons, component/rule ablations, residual errors and token/iteration counts isolate different effects.
findings: The TA-SQL 7B repair-only experiment reduces EF’s remaining execution failures from 72 to 16, a 77.8% reduction, with fewer rounds and tokens. The largest 11.6-point execution-accuracy gain comes from full-pipeline integration. The monitor intercepts all observed out-of-contract proposals in the reported experiments.
limitations: The formal guarantees concern the declared rule family and edit boundaries, not intended semantics or successful repair. Window constructs and some other SQL forms are outside scope; FK-connectivity assumptions are stricter than general SQL validity. Empty results can be legitimate, and selecting the first nonempty replacement column is explicitly heuristic. Mini-Dev overlaps BIRD-Dev, so evaluation settings are not independent corpora.
relevance: A useful mechanism for preventing detectable repair regressions, with a clear boundary between structural verification, semantic correctness and heuristic answer-changing recovery.

claims.claim: Bounded soundness proves that repaired SQL preserves user intent.
claims.evidence: Definition 5 explicitly denies that implication; the loop checks rule violations and edit contracts, and bounded halting can return the last still-invalid state.
claims.disposition: Restrict guarantees to declared properties and finite attempts.

claims.claim: A drop-in repair-only layer yields the headline 11.6-point gain.
claims.evidence: Table 5 uses full-pipeline schema-linking checks; Table 7 is the separately defined repair-only setting. The 77.8% reduction is 72 to 16 in the TA-SQL 7B comparison.
claims.disposition: Keep integration settings and denominators explicit.

claims.claim: Empty-result alignment establishes the correct interpretation.
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 retains predicate operator/literal, selects the first schema-compatible column producing data, and checks static validity; the paper explicitly states this does not certify unstated intent.
claims.disposition: Describe as an optional heuristic rather than answerability or semantic certification.

coverage: All nineteen PDF pages, Sections 1-6, limitations and Appendices A-G, full construction prompts, examples, annotation instructions and result tables; figure captions and main reported results covered.
problem: Conventional SQL benchmarks omit requests needing clarification, missing data or a change to the requested task.
method: PRACTIQ mutates Spider schemas/values or questions into four ambiguous and four unanswerable types. It constructs final SQL first, then reverse-generates clarification replies, with executable-output filtering and LLM quality checks. Some ambiguity types also receive all-options SQL.
evaluation: Few-shot baselines perform nine-way question classification and DIN-SQL generation after receiving the supplied clarification exchange. Classification compares lexical retrieval with oracle cell values. Human review samples question labels and 90 conversations rather than validating every generated dialogue.
findings: Fine-grained classification and post-clarification SQL remain difficult. Missing-information examples often recover by changing the requested attribute/entity, not by discovering information that answers the original request.
limitations: The user is scripted backward from target SQL; the evaluation does not measure agent-led dialogue or repair of imperfect replies. Nonexistent filter values are labeled unanswerable by benchmark convention, which must be distinguished from valid empty/zero results. Printed category counts and aggregate totals disagree.
relevance: Useful for category-specific diagnosis and clarification incorporation with explicit construction and answerability conventions.

claims.claim: Clarification SQL scores measure a complete interactive policy.
claims.evidence: Section 4 supplies the assistant clarification and user reply as generation inputs; Appendices E.4-E.7 sometimes replace the original request with another answerable one.
claims.disposition: Report supplied-dialogue SQL performance, not successful recovery of original intent.

claims.claim: The dataset size is internally consistent.
claims.evidence: Section 3.4 says 1,802 problematic plus 1,034 answerable examples, which sum to 2,836; Table 3 prints total 2,812.
claims.disposition: Use approximately 2,800 unless the released snapshot is independently counted.

claims.claim: Missing filter values make all such SQL requests unanswerable.
claims.evidence: Table 2 and Appendix E.5 define this operational category and replace the missing value in follow-up.
claims.disposition: Preserve benchmark semantics; do not generalize to rejecting every valid empty result.

coverage: All 46 PDF pages: main text and limitations, Appendices A-E, all construction/evaluation prompts, Tables 1-17 and Figures 1-29/case studies. Main behavior/mechanism plots visually checked; garbled figure-text extraction was resolved from page images.
problem: Detect flawed request premises and withhold misleading SQL without suppressing valid paired originals.
method: Creates 1,800 taxonomy-guided perturbation/original pairs and compares Base, Implicit and Explicit flaw prompts. Two judges score ordinal SQL behavior, flaw detection and subtype; separate analyses inspect failure operations.
evaluation: Sixteen models, paired query-level bootstrap comparisons and a 2,160-output human check. Execution validation covers 1,726 originals; GEN itself measures output presence. The 8,000-response mechanism sample excludes unrecoverable schema exposures.
findings: Explicit flaw assertions increase detection but suppress SQL on valid controls. Overt contradictions are easier than ambiguity. Generation and conditional execution quality remain distinct despite their aggregate correlation.
limitations: Taxonomy-derived labels impose a critique policy, not formal SQL impossibility. Mechanism incidence is conditional on selected failures and is unweighted; its 300-example human validation preselects AI-consensus labels, so it is assisted rather than AI-blinded.

problem: SQL-only dialogue fine-tuning can leave systems unable to clarify ambiguous questions, refuse unsupported requests or handle non-database conversation.
method: Combines goal SQL, four thematic relations and four question types to synthesize dialogues; LLM alignment checks, expression refinement and execution checks filter outputs. StateFlow separates intent recognition, SQL generation and execution-error repair.
evaluation: Generates 10,874 dialogues/65,393 turns from SParC and CoSQL training data. Nonanswerable AccS rewards the type label, not response quality. Reported mixed-type CoSQL QM differs between Tables V(50.9) andVI(55.9) without a clear reconciliation.

problem: Detect unsupported or ambiguous biomedical requests before plausible SQL is mistaken for a supported answer.

findings: Balanced demonstrations improve no-answer detection. Execution-error repair removes database errors but can increase incorrect results. Missing values and column ambiguity remain difficult; the interface displays SQL, results and abstention explanations.
limitations: One model and biomedical database, ten negatives per category, reference-result evaluation and a shared negative-demonstration pool limit transfer.
relevance: A concrete refusal-prompting baseline, with useful evidence that executable SQL and successful error repair need not mean correct answers.

problem: Reference-query execution matching can reject plausible interpretations or propagate flawed gold SQL, while an unconstrained LLM judge can accept too much.

problem: Schema-linking models can make confident token errors that propagate into SQL; raw token confidence is insufficient for the studied fine-tuned model.
method: Teacher-forced traces locate branching tokens; layer-specific hidden-state classifiers and conformal prediction sets detect them. Aggregation triggers abstention, a surrogate relevance check or human correction before downstream SQL generation.
evaluation: BIRD and Spider schema-linking and execution metrics with fine-tuned DeepSeek/CodeS models; 20 student participants evaluate 100 sampled questions across expertise levels. The theory concerns marginal prediction-set coverage under calibration assumptions.
findings: Abstention raises linking accuracy among retained cases; human assistance recovers high linking accuracy and improves downstream execution. A surrogate reduces interventions but admits additional errors. Beginners perform worse on difficult column decisions.
limitations: Requires hidden-state access, task-specific labels and a compatible calibration distribution; drift is outside experiments. Human-assisted linking is not autonomous SQL reliability. The draft has reporting inconsistencies: downstream 65.19% is assigned to DeepSeek in prose but CodeS-15B in Table 7, and TAR/FAR formulas reverse the prose conditions.
relevance: Important abstention-at-schema-linking design with bounded statistical claims, not a correctness guarantee for full generated SQL or unknown-intent resolution.

coverage: All seven PDF pages, sections 1–7, equations 1–3 and conformal-set construction, tables 1–2, figures/captions and references; no supplement in the supplied paper.
problem: Schema linking can be correct while the final generated SQL is wrong; the pipeline needs a way to defer uncertain outputs.
method: RTS++ uses RTS schema linking, multiple SQL candidates, decoding probabilities, execution-result clusters, entropy and reranker scores. A calibration quantile forms a candidate set; empty or ambiguous sets trigger abstention or user selection.
evaluation: Spider test and BIRD development results compare reranking, abstention and feedback variants. Calibration uses training data; error tolerance is 0.1 and feedback is assumed accurate. Reported execution accuracy is selective accuracy on the non-abstained subset, accompanied by abstention rates.
findings: Reported accuracy rises when low-confidence cases are withheld, with additional gains under ideal feedback. The headline 92.3%/92.5% values are not full-coverage autonomous accuracy. Removing execution entropy lowers reported reliability and abstention.
limitations: The stated conformal coverage target is not a demonstrated conditional semantic-error guarantee for all executed requests. Candidate completeness and detailed calibration assumptions are not resolved by the short paper. Result normalization ignores some ordering distinctions; warehouse cost and safe execution require separate treatment.
relevance: Useful selective-generation architecture, provided coverage, ideal feedback and database-relative correctness remain explicit.

claims.claim: Headline accuracy establishes general end-to-end reliability.
claims.evidence: Tables 1–2 label selective accuracy and retain 16.1% Spider and 30.6% BIRD abstention with DeepSeek; section 4.1 assumes accurate feedback.
claims.disposition: Limit to the answered subset and ideal-feedback protocol.

claims.evidence: Section 3.3.1 states set coverage over generated candidates; no separate conditional-risk theorem for executed singleton sets is supplied.
claims.disposition: Describe a conformal-calibration proposal and its stated assumptions; do not infer an unconditional semantic guarantee.

version: ORACLE workshop at EMNLP 2026 proceedings, printed pages 84–98
coverage: All 15 pages: sections 1–9, limitations, appendices A–H, threshold/transport formulas, 23 tables, risk-coverage figure and worked candidate example.
problem: An English-calibrated verifier may execute different SQL candidates when only the question language changes, even if aggregate risk remains similar.
method: Generate SQL in English, hold candidate SQL/schema/database/execution label fixed and vary seven-language question renderings. Compare raw thresholds, language-aware score transport and translation-to-English while tracking candidate-level promotions and demotions.
evaluation: Two main 7–8B verifiers score 6,000 candidates; the primary database-disjoint test has 3,005 candidates. Thresholds and corrections are fitted on calibration databases. Clustered bootstrap intervals, repeated split sensitivities and literal-fidelity controls qualify the findings.
findings: Similar ranking metrics and selective risk hide material execution-decision churn. Coverage matching does not restore candidate agreement. Pivot translation reduces several harms more than score transport, but its benefit varies by language, verifier and split and does not recover the English policy.
limitations: English is a reference policy, not truth. Execution labels are instance-specific; complete translation semantics were not manually verified. Generation and schema remain English. Qwen score saturation and precision sensitivity limit threshold transport; some small configuration comparisons are inconclusive.
relevance: Adds decision-transition auditing to aggregate risk/coverage evaluation for multilingual abstention systems.

claims.disposition: Rejected for this protocol; report transitions and fixed denominators.

version: ML4H 2025 manuscript in PMLR volume 297; catalog correctly separates conference year from 2026 proceedings record

problem: A post-generation component must preserve valid SQL, repair erroneous SQL and identify ambiguous or unsupported questions.
method: SCARE balances four categories across three EHR schemas, using candidate SQL from seven generators. Ambiguous/unanswerable questions are model-generated and independently checked by three SQL-proficient annotators. Baselines combine classification, SQL correction, verification and self-refinement.

findings: The main Gemini-2.5-Flash experiments expose preservation-versus-detection trade-offs and weak handling of vague questions/global SQL errors. Appendix A shows substantial backbone-dependent variation; the main-table ambiguity maximum is not the maximum across all tested models.

version: EMNLP 2025 proceedings, pp. 16958–16982, November 4–9, 2025; 25-page published version
coverage: All 25 PDF pages: Sections 1–11, Tables 1–17, Figures 1–5 and their captions, Appendix A supplementary experiments and selected cases, Appendix B feature derivation/Algorithms 1–3, and Appendix C prompts, hyperparameters, compute and license statements. Calibration curves (PDF p.8) and Q-MATCH pseudocode (p.22) visually checked. Both pages of the separately linked responsible-research checklist were also read.
problem: Raw SQL-generation probabilities can be poorly calibrated, limiting their usefulness for identifying likely parser errors.
method: SQLGlot-derived clause matches across nucleus and beam candidates yield frequency features for set operations and two query branches. Their products and the primary output’s token-probability score feed a logistic calibration model. The main setup draws ten candidates by each method; calibration changes confidence, not the selected SQL.
evaluation: T5-PICARD and Llama models are tested on English Spider/BIRD. Spider development data calibrate the test predictions; BIRD uses 1,000 training examples for calibration and 1,534 development examples for testing. Main results use one calibration run, with ten-bin ECE/ACE, Brier score and error-detection AUC; malformed outputs are removed.
findings: MPS improves all four aggregate metrics over ordinary Platt scaling in the four main model/dataset configurations. Improvements are not uniform within difficulty strata. Smaller calibration samples generally weaken performance, and additional generation adds computational cost.
limitations: Representative labeled calibration data are needed; no distribution-shift or selective-risk guarantee is established. The binary correctness evaluator is not identified precisely enough to call the labels execution-match or test-suite labels. Syntactic agreement is not semantic equivalence. A sensitivity discussion inconsistently describes the default sampling budget, and main metrics lack repeated-run uncertainty.
relevance: A practical confidence-calibration baseline for selective SQL answering, distinct from detecting an unanswerable request or validating the user’s intended interpretation.

claims.disposition: Use as empirical confidence/error-ranking evidence under the tested distributions, not an individual-query or abstention guarantee.

coverage: All fourteen PDF pages, Sections 1-8 and Appendices A-H, prompts, graph adaptation, per-domain tables and all example/rubric analyses.
problem: Enterprise terminology and implicit joins can defeat retrieval based only on similarity to poorly documented schemas.
method: The enterprise pipeline mines table usage and joins from query logs, generates metadata/entities, and retrieves through entity matching, graph traversal and ranking. Retrieved metadata, paths and historical examples condition SQL generation.
evaluation: The internal study uses 240 tables, roughly 500,000 logs and 35 test questions, assessed by two engineers and LLM judges. BEAVER evaluates 209 questions but constructs its graph from supplied schema metadata and inferred joins because logs are unavailable.
findings: The BEAVER adaptation improves SQL execution validity from 60.8% to 95.7% over the stated RAG baseline. Pairwise/rubric preference supports better retrieval in tested settings; these are not gold-execution correctness rates.
limitations: Public results do not test log-derived schema discovery. Human-judge agreement is measured on clear-preference internal cases, not all BEAVER judgments. Open-ended question labels and semantic quality scores are model-mediated. Running SQL and receiving high rubric scores do not establish intended answers, complete ambiguity resolution or refusal capability.
relevance: Separates missing documentation from language ambiguity and motivates careful reporting of retrieved-context and evaluation conditions.

claims.claim: 95.7% validates schema-free log-based SQL generation.
claims.evidence: Section 6.1 and Appendix D derive BEAVER metadata from schemas, while the 95.7% metric measures executability.

coverage: All 11 PDF pages: Sections 1-7, Appendices A-B, Tables 1-7 and both figures. Figures 1-2 visually inspected.
problem: Estimate whether a generated query should be answered or withheld, using reference-execution correctness as the target.
method: Compares sampled agreement, probabilities, schema relevance, executability, frozen judges and trained verifiers. Cross-fit logistic calibration combines provider scores; separate calibration/test halves select abstention thresholds.
evaluation: Uses an 800-question, eight-database BIRD convenience slice and 490 multi-table Spider questions. Transfer uses leave-one-database-out evaluation; bootstrap intervals and an additional conservative certificate are reported.
findings: The two-provider ensemble reports AUROC 0.822 and ECE 0.031 on the BIRD slice. Trained verifiers perform better within known schemas than on held-out databases; strong judges outperform sampled agreement in the tested configurations.
limitations: These are dataset/model-specific comparisons, not a universal consistency ceiling. The abstract places statistical signals around 0.61-0.68, but Table 1 lists schema relevance 0.553 and executability 0.500. Figure 1 does not support its caption's claim that the frozen judge leads on every database.
relevance: Separates empirical risk-coverage from certified bounds and candidate correctness from request answerability.

claims.evidence: Table 1 reports 0.553 for schema relevance and 0.500 for executability.
claims.disposition: Overbroad range; only sampled-consistency variants occupy the reported narrow band.

coverage: All 16 PDF pages, sections 1–10, formal contract, route/grain pseudocode, figures 1–2, result/sensitivity tables, threats, code availability and references.
problem: Enterprise SQL can execute while choosing the wrong role, relationship path or aggregation grain.
method: The planner selects question-specific governed semantic identifiers and opaque route handles. Deterministic components review plans, lower roles/grain and compile SQL; known violations block release, while undecidable checker findings do not. One fresh retry is permitted after refusal.
evaluation: One insurance domain compares SPC with DDL-only generation on 38 adjudicated questions, three runs each, with an all-44 sensitivity. LLM judging handles unsettled cases; supersets count as success in the main rule. The six-item exclusion registry was created after inspecting outputs.
findings: The reported system has more questions correct on all three runs and fewer adjudicated wrong-but-executed outcomes. Strict-equivalence and all-item sensitivities retain the direction. Targeted multiplicity counterfactuals expose known fan-trap defects.
limitations: The compiler was developed on this benchmark; semantic knowledge, retry allowance and possibly sampling differ between arms. Judging is not independently human-validated. Public code excludes evaluation databases, verdicts and exact campaign state, preventing full reproduction. Deterministic compilation does not guarantee a correct business interpretation.
relevance: A bounded architecture case study, useful for separating reproducible relational construction from uncertain semantic selection.

version: arXiv:2610.04156v1, 2 October 2026; manuscript reports a Resource-Aware Agentic AI workshop
coverage: All 19 pages, Sections 1-6, Appendices A-M, decision equations, Tables 1-9, figure captions, prompts and complete example trajectory.
problem: Clinical SQL agents can spend multiple steps producing plausible incorrect answers or answering questions unsupported by the database.
method: Two per-agent ModernBERT classifiers score question/trajectory prefixes for answerability and eventual correctness. Calibration selects early-exit thresholds and delivery-time Chow-style withholding, optionally combining transcript scores with execution/schema features.
evaluation: Five fixed ReAct agents on template-disjoint pools constructed from EHRSQL/MIMIC-III training and validation data. Primary correctness uses GPT-4o-mini judgments after strict mismatches; template-cluster intervals and strict-label sensitivity are reported.
findings: At low error penalty the monitor improves utility over always abstaining for four of five agents while reducing coverage. At higher penalties results are statistically comparable to refusing everything. Early stopping saves agent steps, but reported savings exclude monitor inference overhead.
limitations: One database and mostly one seed; monitors need agent-specific trajectories. A human audit finds judge disagreement on 26% of adjudicated hard cases. Question-only shortcuts nearly solve answerability, and strict execution labels substantially reduce gains. No competing confidence implementation is evaluated.
relevance: Clarifies trade-offs among refusal, correctness, coverage and compute; benchmark utility is not evidence of safe clinical deployment.

claims.claim: Sentinel yields reliable high-stakes answers.
claims.evidence: Appendix F finds gains over always-refuse indistinguishable from zero at medium/high penalties; coverage is very low.
claims.disposition: A useful abstention verdict rather than demonstrated high-coverage clinical reliability.

claims.disposition: Gross agent-call savings, not measured net end-to-end resource savings.

claims.disposition: Near-balanced errors in this selected audit do not establish unbiasedness outside it; label uncertainty affects results.

coverage: All 15 PDF pages, sections 1–5, limitations/ethics, references and appendices A–B; tables 1–5 and rendered figures 2–3/table 1 inspected.
problem: Repeated generation agreement is a potential confidence signal, but the relation between agreement and correctness needs a calibrated mapping.
method: SIMBA aggregates pairwise similarities through arithmetic averaging, a conditional-independence Bayesian model or supervised random forests. Some variants add log-probability features and therefore are not entirely black-box.
evaluation: Nine datasets cover QA, summarization and SQL. SQL uses CodeLlama/Granite outputs on Spider, Spider-Realistic and BIRD, labeled by execution agreement. Five random half-training/half-test splits evaluate calibration error, top-selection accuracy and AUROC; lower-temperature generations are the main scored outputs.
findings: Learned aggregation improves calibration in the reported in-domain settings; top-selection and AUROC gains can be modest, and Bayesian aggregation sometimes calibrates poorly. Error bars are min/max across five runs, not confidence intervals.
limitations: Results assume stable sampling and suitable in-domain labeled examples; schema-disjoint calibration transfer is not established. Appendix B has ambiguous sample-count wording. Several non-SQL p(true) ACE cells exceed one despite the probability-based definition, so those numerical comparisons require clarification.
relevance: Useful confidence-estimation baselines; calibration is distinct from semantic equivalence, input answerability and a guarantee for individual predictions.

claims.claim: Improved calibration implies strong correctness discrimination.
claims.evidence: Conclusion and Appendix B explicitly characterize ATS/AUROC gains as moderate or marginal; Table 1 separates these metrics.
claims.disposition: Keep calibration improvements separate from answer selection and rejection quality.

claims.locator: Section 4.1, printed page 15885; rendered Table 1, page 15886
claims.disposition: Reporting/normalization ambiguity remains; do not rely on those cells for quantitative comparisons.

coverage: All 34 pages: sections 1–6, references, Appendices A–M, both algorithms, complete prompts, proof and end-to-end example; Figure 1 visually inspected.
problem: Underspecified intent, overlapping schema meanings and missing business context can produce plausible but semantically misaligned SQL.
method: The system creates ten plan-generate-critique candidates, derives ambiguity dimensions from disagreement and a taxonomy, executes targeted probes and repairs a selected seed. Optional synthetic clarification examples are generated from SQL-log anchors and retrieved into generation.
evaluation: Three backbones are compared with AutoLink and DeepEye-SQL on five benchmark partitions, plus a 300-example AMBROSIA study. Separate experiments add synthetic logs derived from provided benchmark gold SQLs. Fifty artifact-complete Spider cases receive a model-judge audit of probe grounding, resolution and repair.
findings: No-log execution accuracy improves across the reported settings, and probing recovers cases missed by candidate selection. The synthetic-log condition improves further, but has different supervision. The AMBROSIA result measures the chosen execution outcome, not comprehensive interpretation coverage or user-validated intent recovery.
limitations: The paper does not clearly establish a disjoint historical-log/evaluation split for gold-derived clarifications. Larger or more coherent probe results do not identify a user’s unstated preference. The information-theoretic proposition assumes a conditional Markov relation and gives an upper bound, not an empirical guarantee of correct clarification. Candidate diversity, judge validity and added inference cost remain boundaries.
relevance: A useful autonomous probing design, provided evidence about database feasibility is distinguished from evidence of intended business meaning and gold-derived supervision is reported separately.

claims.claim: The query-log setting uses only independent historical evidence.
claims.evidence: Section 4.3 explicitly uses provided dataset gold SQLs as intent anchors; it says raw gold is not exposed but gives no clear disjointness protocol for derived clarification records.

coverage: All 22 pages, main sections 1–10, limitations, references, Appendices A–G and all example rows; plotted main results and generator/rewrite figures visually inspected.
problem: Executable answers can silently settle consequential calculation choices. Single-reference evaluation cannot distinguish an inability to compute an interpretation from failure to disclose or return an interpretation the model can compute.
method: SpecBridge constructs matched open/A-specific/B-specific requests on existing databases, holding other requirements fixed. Executed references distinguish the two interpretations; reviewers and two authors screen the triples. Decide-then-answer enumerates choices before separate generation calls and preserves the original request when adding a user’s choice.
evaluation: The main study uses 204 accepted triples across 12 databases, four models, AMBROSIA and selected BIRD cases. Computation uses execution matching; explanation labels use a model judge. The method comparison uses two models and includes a simulated two-turn user.
findings: Among triples where both specific requests are computable, models return both interpretations for only 15–58% of open requests. Deciding first improves coverage over a single-answer baseline; preserving wording reduces losses caused by rewriting unrelated formulas, columns or joins.
limitations: Tests cover one controlled choice and two references, not all interpretations or natural traffic. Open-request outputs outside those references are not penalized; precision is measured on clear requests. Product behavior is reconstructed from documentation, not tested live. User simulation assumes reliable interpretation recognition, and the clause-addition comparison was added after an interim look.
relevance: A useful mechanism-focused benchmark for separating SQL capability from disclosure and for testing clarification edits that preserve all other intent constraints.

problem: Conventional SQL benchmarks underrepresent large schemas, dialect differences, external business definitions and repository-level data transformation workflows.

problem: Users may identify errors in an initial query through plain-language explanations without being able to edit SQL directly.

relevance: A useful controlled test of incorporating feedback, with a different objective from choosing clarification questions or refusing unsupported requests.

problem: Two SQL queries can agree on a benchmark database while differing on another valid instance; conversely, a gold query may itself be wrong or represent only one plausible interpretation.
method: SpotIt extends VeriEQL with string/date operations and type conversions, searches successively larger bounded symbolic databases, validates generated counterexamples in the backend and optionally cross-checks counterexamples across systems.
evaluation: Ten systems are re-evaluated on 1,533 BIRD development questions, searching primarily execution-passing pairs up to five rows per relation with 600-second verifier limits. Additional tests cover 135 SQLite Spider 2.0 questions and a manual sample of 50 CSC-32B discrepancies.
findings: The verifier supports roughly 94–97% of BIRD execution-passing pairs and finds additional differences that change rankings. In the 50-case audit, 64% are attributed to problematic gold SQL, 26% to predictions and 10% to ambiguity; these are discrepancy-sample proportions.
limitations: Counterexamples establish query disagreement, not which interpretation satisfies the user. No-counterexample results may reflect bounds, unsupported syntax or timeout. Runtime averages below four seconds cover successful counterexample cases. Window functions, recursive queries and ordering nondeterminism remain limitations; some appendix examples have semantic inconsistencies requiring care before reuse.
relevance: Strong evidence for separating reference equivalence from natural-language correctness, and for inspecting small counterexamples when auditing benchmark labels or accepting generated SQL.
